News.title: Russia could attack Nato within WEEKS, US intelligence warns as Putin ‘aims to test alliance amid weapons shortage’
News.content:
RUSSIA could attack Nato within weeks, according to new US intelligence reports.

US officials fear Vladimir Putin is plotting a small-scale land incursion to test the alliance as he faces daily humiliating attacks on his doorstep.



Until now, US intelligence believed Putin would not risk provoking Nato while fighting in Ukraine.

But the assessment has changed this year, The Wall Street Journal reports.





Possible threats include a cyberattack on a Nato country, sending armed groups to occupy territory or a limited incursion on the alliance’s eastern flank.

Putin could test Nato with a possible attack at any point between autumn this year and 2029, the report said.

One theory is Putin could grab a city in Poland, or one of the three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, all Nato nations which have strongly backed Ukraine during the war.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda warned recently: “I cannot deny that we have such information and that it concerns kinetic operations.



“Not on a large scale, but targeted kinetic operations that are very likely to be directed against critical infrastructure.”

And on Thursday, Lithuania’s defence minister said Russia is planning to use Ukrainian-made drones to attack the Baltics in a “false flag” hit.

Russian opposition politician Garry Kasparov believes Putin will launch a “small incursion” into Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania or Poland.



He added: “I think the chances are growing because Putin needs a winning narrative and Ukraine doesn’t offer it.”

Putin might try to grab limited Nato territory in the Baltics to claim he has scored a victory against the West.

All three Baltic states have strengthened their border defences against Russia and close ally Belarus.

Nato spokesman Colonel Martin O’Donnell said: “We are always thinking through and preparing for any number of scenarios.

“Nato is watching and we are ready to deter and defend as necessary.”



A land incursion has previously been considered highly unlikely as it would trigger Nato’s Article 5 – meanig an attack against one ally is considered an attack against all members.

Nato members believe Putin is already conducting probing attacks to test the alliance.



This includes Russian drones flying into Romania.

The Nato member has faced dozens of incursions by unmanned aerial vehicles since the outbreak of Russia‘s war in Ukraine.

Recently, Western fighter jets have been scrambled three times to shoot down drones.

Fighter jets were scrambled 250 per cent more in July compared with a year ago as Russia probes the West’s defences.



“The numbers do not lie,” NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said.

And just days ago, an explosives-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in a possible Russian provocation.

Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to inspect the drone and found it had been equipped with professional explosives and a detonator.

If it had exploded then the blast could have not only injured those nearby but also set light to the aircraft, its fuel and the ammo inside.



In Lithuania, air raid alerts were issued earlier this year after a drone flew close to the border in neighbouring Belarus.

The US intelligence assessment comes amid US concern about a shortfall of munitions after supplies to Ukraine and use in the Middle East conflict.

But Trump hit back at reports of weapons shortages, saying: “The US has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types.

“Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed.”



Wes Streeting this week warned that Russian provocations against the UK were just the “tip of the iceberg”.

On his first day as Defence Secretary a Russian warship opened fire as it steamed towards the Channel.

The frigate Neustrashimy spent 30 minutes blasting shells as big as traffic bollards into waters off the coast of Plymouth.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He told The Sun: “Incidents like the shooting in the Channel are performative, irresponsible and designed to provoke.

“It does at least provide the British with a visible manifestation of the provocations we see from Russia every day.”

News.title: Moment hero cafe owner plunges into sea fully clothed to save three screaming children from choppy waves at UK beach
News.content:
A CAFE owner has been hailed a hero after plunging into the rough sea fully clothed to save three children.

The chef rescued screaming kids from choppy waves off the Kent Coast on Wednesday.



Former Royal Marine Steven Doorey-Williams, 56, was working in the kitchen at Bayside Cafe at Dumpton Gap beach near Broadstairs when he heard screams coming from the water.

He ran outside and saw two boys and a girl struggling in the sea.



Steven immediately grabbed a buoyancy ring and waded into the water fully clothed, before bringing the children back to safety one by one.

The footage shows the hero dragging the kids through the choppy water into the shore.



Local resident Jo Drake, who witnessed the rescue outside the café, said Steven had been cooking when the incident unfolded.

She said: “I walked past his kitchen and saw him cooking then as I walked on it became apparent these children were in trouble.

“He didn’t hesitate when he heard the screaming. He just waded in fully clothed and rescued the children.

“He’s a hero.”



Fellow witness Andy Milnes also saw the incident and praised Steven for his quick response.

He said: “I saw the whole incident. Steve was there immediately and assisted all three kids ashore.”

Steven, who is also a retired firefighter, was praised by other locals following the dramatic rescue.

Amanda Rooke said: “Well done Steve, fantastic response and bravery.”

Another witness, Michelle Hallissey, added: “What a hero. Well done for saving these children, amazing.”

News.title: From Thames Water to South West Water, full list of hosepipe bans in the UK – and if there’s one in your area
News.content:
MILLIONS of Brits are facing water restrictions this weekend as another hosepipe ban comes into force.

Half of England is in drought conditions following a prolonged spell of dry, hot weather, and many water companies have now taken measures in response.



From Saturday August 8, South West Water is introducing a hosepipe ban that will impact around 1.8million people.

It means all domestic customers across Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly will be banned from using a hose.



South West Water already had a ban in place for Mid and East Devon, but this new measure will see almost the entire South West region face restrictions from 12.01am on Saturday.

Nine water companies have now introduced bans across the UK, affecting over 23million customers in total – here’s everything you need to know.

Which suppliers have put hosepipe bans in place?

If you live in any of the following regions, you are currently subject to a hosepipe ban:

Affinity Water: The Central region, covering Bedfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, Surrey, and parts of London and Essex.

The Central region, covering Bedfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, Surrey, and parts of London and Essex. Anglian Water: The whole supply region.

The whole supply region. Cambridge Water: The whole supply region.

The whole supply region. Dwr Cymru Welsh Water: Mid and South Ceredigion, North Pembrokeshire, and North Carmarthenshire.

Mid and South Ceredigion, North Pembrokeshire, and North Carmarthenshire. Essex and Suffolk Water: All household customers across the supply area.

All household customers across the supply area. South East Water: Kent, Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire, and Berkshire.

Kent, Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire, and Berkshire. South West Water: Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly (from Saturday August 8). Mid and East Devon are already under restrictions.

Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly (from Saturday August 8). Mid and East Devon are already under restrictions. Southern Water: Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Thames Water: The entire supply area, including Greater London, the Thames Valley, Surrey, Gloucestershire, and North Wiltshire.

Is there a hosepipe ban in my area?

If you’re unsure who your water supplier is, or whether your specific street is included in the ban, the easiest way to check is online.

Visit your water supplier’s website and enter your postcode into their designated hosepipe ban checker to find out if a hosepipe ban applies to your home.

What are the rules of a hosepipe ban?

Under a Temporary Use Ban (TUB), you cannot use a hosepipe, sprinkler, or pressure washer for a variety of domestic tasks. This includes:



Watering your garden, plants, or lawn.

Cleaning your car, patio, or driveway.

Filling up a paddling pool, swimming pool, or hot tub.

Cleaning external walls or windows.

You can still carry out most of these activities if you use tap water from a bucket or watering can.

You can also use water not sourced from the mains, such as grey water (leftover bath or sink water) or rainwater collected in a water butt.

Anyone caught breaking these temporary rules can face a hefty £1,000 fine, unless they have an approved exemption or loophole in place.

Who is exempt?

Most water companies offer exemptions for some vulnerable customers.

Those on the Priority Services Register, disabled people, and Blue Badge holders who may struggle to carry heavy buckets or watering cans are generally permitted to continue using a hose for essential tasks.



To check if you’re exempt from hosepipe ban restrictions, visit your water supplier’s website to view their exemption criteria or contact their customer service team.

Why are bans being introduced?

Half of England and the entirety of Wales are currently under official drought conditions.

Sam Bottomley of South West Water explained that “exceptionally low rainfall” and “high demand during warmer weather” had provoked the decision to roll out the new restrictions.

He said: “Introducing a hosepipe ban is never a decision we take lightly, and we fully appreciate the inconvenience it will cause.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“However, these temporary restrictions are an important step in helping to protect our rivers and essential water supplies for homes, businesses and critical services across the region.”



Customers are also being urged to use less water by taking shorter showers, turning off the tap when brushing their teeth, and ensuring washing machines and dishwashers are only run on full loads.

News.title: Chilling moment balaclava-clad gunmen warn tourists to stay away from Brit getaway island & threaten holiday homeowners
News.content:
THIS is the chilling moment balaclava-clad gunmen threaten tourists and demand they stay away from a beloved Brit getaway destination.

Corsican separatists have issued a terrifying warning telling holidaymakers they won’t be “safe” if they move to the island or consider buying second homes.



Chilling footage showed around a dozen armed members of the Corsican National Liberation Front-Union of Combatants (FLNC-UC) addressing tourists.

Wielding submachine guns and sniper rifles, the hooded combatants said through distorted audio: “Until our national rights are recognised and respected, we have only one message for them: stay at home.



“The Corsican people will never be a vulgar administrative community.”

The gang released the video after holding a clandestine press conference for only a single local media outlet known as Corse Matin.



Corsica, a rugged mountainous island in the Mediterranean Sea with a population of around 365,000, is an official region of France and the birthplace of Emperor Napoleon.

Its turquoise seas and picturesque sandy beaches help attract thousands of visitors each year with many choosing to stay.

Corsica has even been home to a row of billionaires such as Princess Caroline of Monaco, Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, Mick Jagger and Bill Gates.

In the last decade, Corsica’s population rose by 32,900 – an average growth of one per cent a year – according to the country’s national statistics office INSEE.



6 Credit: Getty Images/Radius Images

The rising number of people has sparked a boom in the housing market as thousands also chose the island to buy a second home on.

FLNC-UC’s leader warned that anyone buying a holiday home from now on would be considered a threat.

They attacked the flow of 5,000 foreigners, which they say the vast majority are French, of causing “rampant settlement-driven colonisation”.



The masked militant boss said he is being forced to step in to avoid the Corsican population being “wiped out”.

The threat came as the separatists continue to fight for greater autonomy for Corsica.

A bill was adopted by the lower house in June which would give Corsica special autonomous status but remain a French administrative region.



At the time Françoise Gatel, the minister of decentralisation, called it “an important step for Corsica and for our democracy”.

But the FLNC-UC separatist group claims the proposed law won’t go far enough in guaranteeing Corsican independence.

France’s National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office has now opened a preliminary investigation over the footage.

They are looking if it breaches “criminal conspiracy to prepare acts of terrorism” laws.

The acquisition, possession and transport of weapons, ammunition or weapons elements in relation to a terrorist enterprise is also being considered.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Corsican separatists have been active since the 1970s.

They became known across the Mediterranean in 1976 when they claimed responsibility for 18 attacks – mainly bombings – carried out across one night.

News.title: Fury as oblivious tourists pose for photos on edge of crumbling & ‘extremely unstable’ 170ft cliff in UK seaside town
News.content:
CLIFF HANGERS Fury as oblivious tourists pose for photos on edge of crumbling & ‘extremely unstable’ 170ft cliff in UK seaside town

FURIOUS locals have blasted tourists for posing for photos on the edge of a crumbling 170ft cliff despite warnings it could collapse at any moment.

Shocking images show adults and children standing just inches from the cliff edge at Seaford Head in East Sussex.



Other pictures capture sightseers smiling for selfies on the brink of the chalk cliffs, having appeared to ignore warning signs and visible cracks in the ground.

The beauty spot overlooks the famous Seven Sisters cliffs and attracts thousands of walkers every year.



But the dramatic coastline is also one of Britain’s most dangerous.

The white chalk cliffs are riddled with deep tension cracks and huge sections regularly break away and crash onto the beach below.



Visitors are urged to stay at least five metres back from the edge while taking in the views.

Despite that, more than a dozen people were seen venturing dangerously close for photographs.



East Sussex County Council has repeatedly warned the cliffs are “extremely unstable”.

A council statement says: “Every year, thousands of tons of chalk falls from the cliffs.

“Despite warning signs, people often stand near the edge. Chalk cliffs are extremely unstable and can fall at any time.

“People underestimate the risks they are taking.”

The danger has become so severe that even the nearby Seaford Head Golf Course is being forced to change its layout.



Parts of the historic links course sit beside the eroding cliff edge and repeated collapses have left golfers playing dangerously close to the drop.

The club now plans to move its famous 18th tee and 17th green as a safety measure.

The spectacular 18th tee stands around 300ft above sea level and is regarded as one of the most photographed tee shots in British golf.



But recent cliff falls, including one that sent hundreds of tonnes of chalk crashing onto the beach, have left its future in doubt.

Simon Lambert, the course manager who has worked at Seaford Head Golf Course for 26 years, said the changes were needed to protect everyone using the site.

He said: “It’s for the safety of all users – golfers, walkers and anyone else using the site or the path – and to future proof the 18-hole course.

“Coastal erosion has been a big factor to consider for a number of years now here on Seaford Head.

“We have seen a number of smaller and some more significant cliff falls over time.



“It is something that is happening with ever increasing extremes of weather both wet and dry and I feel this will only continue and we need to be proactively working towards managing the effects of what seems to be an unstoppable issue.”

The 17th green also lies partly within a 2,500-year-old Iron Age hill fort, with parts of the ancient monument already lost to the sea.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A major collapse in 2021 led to the site being added to Historic England‘s Heritage at Risk register.

Plans to move parts of the course will now be considered by organisations including South Downs National Park, Natural England and Historic England before any final decision is made.

News.title: Detective sacked after branding ‘all men’ rapists who should have 9pm curfews & calling trans women ‘c***s in frocks’
News.content:
COP ROW Detective sacked after branding ‘all men’ rapists who should have 9pm curfews & calling trans women ‘c***s in frocks’

A DETECTIVE who told colleagues “all men are rapists” and should face a 9pm curfew has been sacked following a gross misconduct probe.

Rachel Fletcher has been axed from Northumbria Police after also describing transgender women as “c**ks in frocks”, a panel heard.



It was also heard that Fletcher, who worked in the force’s safeguarding unit, said “no wonder a f***ing man did it”, while talking about a crime.

Det Con Fletcher made the “inappropriate” comments about men and trans women to colleagues over an 11-month period.



A panel at Houghton police station near Sunderland, Tyne and Wear, found that she had made all of the alleged comments.

It heard she breached Standards of Professional Behaviour in relation to discreditable conduct, authority, respect and courtesy and equality and diversity.

Barrister Olivia Checa-Dover said Fletcher had been accused of making comments about men in which she “expressed hatred”.

She told the panel that Fletcher had made junior male colleagues feel intimidated and uncomfortable, but had showed no remorse.

DC Fletcher admitted saying, “the only way to stop night time rapes is to put a 9 o’clock curfew on all men”, or something similar, as a joke.

She said: “I wouldn’t have said all men are rapists because I don’t believe that all men are rapists. I mentioned the male curfew as a joke.



“It’s not a proposition that I would support in reality. It was in an office with colleagues all dealing with the same horrible things I do on a day to day basis.

“It was a flippant remark in a much more serious conversation.”

In January 2024, Fletcher also referred to transgender women as “c**ks in frocks” during a conversation about strip searches.

Ms Checa-Dover added: “There is no doubt that violence against women and girls is a police priority, and a significant public concern.

“A police officer asserting that all men should be on a curfew damages efforts to promote public confidence.



“If a male police officer made a blanket statement about women, he would be held to account.”

Giving evidence, PC Kevin Thompson claimed he joked about Fletcher’s views on men at first, but later felt intimidated.

PC Thompson told the panel, chaired by Assistant Chief Constable Andy Hill, that Fletcher had a habit of making her views known.

He said :”If a man was saying these things about a woman, they would be dealt with. It just made me feel uncomfortable.”

Sergeant Damon Hall overheard Fletcher laughing while discussing a curfew for men with another colleague in December 2023.



He said: “Knowing Fletcher as I do, I know she has a sharp wit.

“There was a certain amount of tongue and cheek in what she said.

“In hindsight, I probably should have challenged it, maybe I missed the boat a little bit there.”

DC Barbara Callaghan confirmed she worked with Fletcher in safeguarding.

She told the panel they “got on really well”, and had a “warm and friendly relationship”.



But it was during their time working together that DC Fletcher was accused of making a comment about “c***ks in frocks”.

DC Callaghan said new policy was set to be introduced meaning female officers would be obligated to search transgender women.

She told the panel that news of the policy had “upset” Fletcher.

Naomi Cunningham, for DC Fletcher, said the rules had included intimate searches, which should have been recognised as unlawful.

She said: “It took the supreme court to make that clear but it shouldn’t have taken the supreme court to make that clear”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

ACC Hill said the panel had taken into account her important work, as well as character witnesses describing her as kind, hardworking and diligent.

But he added the only appropriate outcome would be to dismiss Fletcher without notice, saying: “The officer will be placed on the barred list.”

News.title: Dad, 42, left with 100 shrapnel pieces in head after being shot when thugs broke down door & mistook him for gang rival
News.content:
WRONG TARGET Dad, 42, left with 100 shrapnel pieces in head after being shot when thugs broke down door & mistook him for gang rival

A DAD was shot in the head in his own home and left with 100 pieces of shrapnel in his forehead by gang members who targeted the wrong house.

Jason Franklin, 42, was enjoying a quiet night in with his partner Keela, 36, and their five-month-old son Lucas, when intruders attempted to break down their front door before firing through the glass panel.



The dad-of-four from Bristol was left with a hole in his head and shards of glass in his eyes after the brutal attack.

Cops told Jason that he had been caught in the crossfire of a feud between rival gangs, who had mistakenly turned up at his property.



But his attackers have never been found, and police closed the investigation after a few months, having exhausted all lines of enquiry.

The fencer – who is currently unable to work due to mental health struggles – said he is devastated that those responsible were never caught.

He described the lasting impact on his mental health as horrible, adding that it is terrible there have been no repercussions.

“I’ve got PTSD, anxiety, depression; it’s really affected Lucas as I wasn’t able to take him out to places when he was growing up, due to my mental health,” he said.

“We’ve not been able to live like a normal family.”

On the evening of Easter Sunday, April 4, 2010, the couple were on the sofa in their Ashley Wood home watching a film while Lucas slept in his pram nearby.



At around 10pm, Keela went upstairs to put Lucas in his cot before returning downstairs while Jason drifted off on the sofa – but just half an hour later, he was jolted awake by a loud banging noise.

Confused and terrified, he ran to the front door and pressed his body against it to keep the intruders out.

He admitted he had no idea who it could be or why anyone would try to break into his home.



Suddenly, a loud bang echoed through the hallway accompanied by the smell of smoke.

The glass panels in the door shattered as a bullet struck Jason directly in the top of his head.

“The intruders couldn’t get through the door, so they decided to just shoot through the glass,” he said.

As blood poured from his head, he ran upstairs to grab a towel, leaving bloody handprints along the walls.

Keela dialed 999 immediately as the intruders fled into the night.



Jason was rushed to hospital, where he received 10 stitches and underwent surgery to remove shards of glass from his eyes.

“When they shot me in the head, it damaged the nerve, so I couldn’t feel much, but my eyes were in so much pain,” he said.

Detectives informed the family that the attackers had used a homemade bullet, which shattered on impact and left 100 pieces of shrapnel in his forehead.



Doctors advised against removing the fragments, explaining that doing so would only worsen the scarring.

“You can still feel little bits of metal if you touch my head in certain places,” he said.

Officers revealed the assault stemmed from a dispute between rival gangs who had targeted the wrong address.

“They didn’t do their research; they were just told to go to the house next to the boarded-up house, but they got the wrong side,” Jason said.

After five days in hospital, Jason was discharged to his mother’s house, four doors down from the crime scene, where his family was staying.



Two months later, they relocated to a flat on the other side of Bristol to regain a sense of safety but cops later closed the case after running out of leads, leaving Jason devastated.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The random attack severely damaged his mental health, leaving him struggling to leave the house or take his children out in the years that followed.

Avon & Somerset Police has been contacted for comment.

News.title: Heart-stopping moment boy, 12, is dragged under giant lorry – but miraculously WALKS AWAY unharmed
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a 12-year-old boy is sent flying beneath the wheels of a massive lorry – but miraculously stands up and walks away.

The youngster had been wheeling his bicycle along Avenida Joaquim David in Brazil before his jacket suddenly snagged on a passing truck.



Heart-stopping footage shows the schoolchild being dragged under the massive tyres as his bicycle is flung aside.

The terrifying incident unfolded in Firminopolis, central Brazil on Wednesday.



The Volvo FH 540 had been turning onto the GO-060 highway while the boy had been making his way home from school.

Several carriages of the massive truck wheeled past the child until he became hooked and was sent him flying beneath the wheels.



His body appeared to have been dragged along the tarmac by the huge multi-wheeler.

Miraculously, the youngster was not crushed by the truck – and stood up and walked away.

Staff from a nearby chemist raced to the scene and gave the boy first aid.

The driver did not stop at the scene.



The boy suffered a fracture to his left wrist and some grazing on his elbow, according to medics at Hospital Santa Gemma.

He will undergo surgery after being transported to the Goias State Emergency Hospital Dr Valdemiro Cruz (Hugol) in Goiania.

The driver reportedly only found out about the crash when a friend sent him a video of the collision.



He contacted the Military Police and explained that he drove off because he had no idea that he had hit anyone.

The child had been standing in a blind spot behind his mirror, he said.

The truck driver asked police for the contact details of the mother.

He said he would support the family and offered to meet the costs of the boy’s medical treatment.

Cops are investigating the incident.

News.title: Academics call for independent inquiry into Jason Arday's Cambridge appointment
News.content:
A group of academics is calling for an independent investigation into the appointment of Prof Jason Arday, who resigned from his University of Cambridge roles following allegations of plagiarism.

The former chair of the education faculty has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work.

Attention has now turned to Cambridge's handling of concerns about Arday, who became its youngest-ever black professor in 2023.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Cambridge announced on Thursday that it had begun an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

But Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic roles have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus" which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

The BBC has approached the University of Cambridge and LJMU for comment.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, he said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the unrest had "put Thetford back decades" after years of trying to improve the town's reputation.

Speaking to the BBC on Friday, he said: "It's been awful the last few nights, it's been terrifying for many Thetford residents."

He said he had been made aware of properties being "pelted with eggs" on Thursday and said the town was "on edge".

He said the violence was "scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked".

He urged fellow politicians to "call out" the violent protests and assaults of police officers.

Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks â including at RAF Barnham, near Thetford.

The town's mayor, Vic Peters, said he supported peaceful protests but condemned "willful disregard of the law".

Commenting as an individual and not on behalf of the town council, he said council staff had been subjected to abuse and intimidation and councillors have been verbally abused in the past week.

Scott Hussey, a Reform councillor for the nearby Brecks division on Norfolk County Council, said a "peaceful protest" had started at the town's police station on Wednesday night before it moved to Clover Way.

He described the protest as "spirited" and said there had been "some skirmishes" but said he saw no violence.

He accused the Home Office of "opening a number of these HMOs across Thetford" and "trying to rush through the site for asylum seekers at Barnham".

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

They acknowledged concerns about immigration in Thetford but condemned the violence of some protesters.

A spokesperson said: "The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and the concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms."

News.title: How a diary entry solved the murder of a missing man
News.content:
When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.

Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany.

"He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled.

"It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."

Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.

The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.

His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.

Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan.

"We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.

On 28 July, Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family.

At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

But how did police finally catch them?

News.title: Norway call for Infantino to resign as Mexico and Argentina back president
News.content:
Norway have called on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, but Mexico and Argentina have voiced their support for the 56-year-old.

Norway have gone a step further than the football associations of England, Wales, Croatia and Albania, all of whom have withdrawn support for Infantino without explicitly calling for him to resign.

"He [Infantino] does not have the institutional trust required to govern Fifa stably in the times we are in," Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said on Friday.

"There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in trouble, and we must have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the Fifa president to resign now.

"We will see which other countries eventually join in, if that becomes the strategy from the Uefa board. We are not going to ask for an extraordinary [Uefa board] meeting, we will ask him to resign in our dialogue with Fifa."

Klaveness, who is a qualified lawyer, went through a list of concerns that the Norwegian FA has expressed to Fifa during her four-year tenure.

Among them were questions around the awarding of tournaments, the inaugural Fifa peace prize that was awarded to US President âDonald Trump in December, and the overturning of a ban for American forward Folarin Balogun during the recent World Cup following a phone call from Trump.

Meanwhile, earlier on Friday the Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, called for a "comprehensive reckoning" of Infantino's presidency after he aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

However, 2026 World Cup co-hosts Mexico have backed Infantino's leadership amid widespread calls for him to resign.

"The FMF [Mexican FA] supports president Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening," a statement read.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa members.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made by president Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations," it added.

News.title: Divers find 162-year-old Guinness in shipwreck off the English coast
News.content:
How far would you travel for a pint of Guinness? If the answer is to the bottom of the sea, you might be in luck.

There's just one catch - the pint in question is 162 years old.

When Belgian underwater photographer Stefan Panis discovered a bottle buried in a shipwreck off the coast of Dover in 2025, he had no idea what he had found. He just knew something about it had caught his eye.

When Panis and his friend, Eddie Huzzey, surfaced, a quick rinse revealed the familiar Guinness branding. The bottle dates back to 1864.

"We lifted the artefact, and then on the surface a quick rinse revealed 'Guinness'," he said.

News.title: NHS Tayside investigates data breach into Minnie Merriman medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe in Arbroath.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town.

A 35-year-old man, who was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added : "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after major search launched at beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search operation was launched after concerns were raised for a young girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park near Gorebridge at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A force spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

Police said her family were aware.

News.title: Sullivan set to attend West Ham tie against advice
News.content:
West Ham are expecting David Sullivan to attend Saturday's Carabao Cup first-round tie against Portsmouth despite him being advised to stay away from home matches at London Stadium.

Sullivan, 77, resigned from his position as co-chair of West Ham in June after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour.

He has categorically denied the allegations.

On Monday, a spokesperson for London Stadium told BBC News it had "recommended" to West Ham that Sullivan does not attend matches because of concerns about fan unrest.

London Stadium has asked for advance notice of any planned visits by major shareholder Sullivan - who retains a 38.8% stake in the club - in order to implement additional safety and operational measures.

The match against Portsmouth will be the first the club has played since the allegations against Sullivan were first reported.

The Panorama and Times joint investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for the past three years because of safeguarding concerns.

London Stadium was unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historical allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false.

Sullivan had already been the subject of intense fan abuse for his running of the club, who were relegated to the Championship last season for the first time since 2011.

Although West Ham have stabilised on the pitch, with key figures, including manager Nuno Espirito Santo and skipper Jarrod Bowen committing their future to the club, there remains huge uncertainty off it.

Vanessa Gold, daughter of Sullivan's late business partner and former West Ham co-chair David, backed out of a deal to sell part of her stake in the club to Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky, and instead reached an agreement with Amanda Staveley, the public face of the Saudi Arabia-backed takeover at Newcastle, to sell her entire 25.1% stake.

However, Kretinsky has since sold a small part of his own stake, bringing him under 25%.

That would allow him to buy Gold's shares under West Ham's pre-emption rights rules - which allow existing shareholders first choice to buy shares when they become available.

If he did so he would become West Ham's biggest shareholder, without triggering another clause that would force him to then buy the rest of the club.

It is anticipated Saturday's match against fellow Championship side Portsmouth (15:00 BST) will set an attendance record for an EFL Cup first-round tie, with the Hammers having sold 55,000 season tickets for the new campaign.

News.title: Man 'humiliated' after being told mobility scooter too big for train
News.content:
A man with osteoarthritis and learning difficulties has said he feels "humiliated" after being told he cannot take his new mobility scooter on Translink's train services because it has been deemed to be too big.

Stephen Magee had been using his previous scooter for about five years without any problems.

But he said after Translink assessed his new scooter he was told it is 10cm too large.

A Translink spokesperson said the company was committed to providing accessible services for everyone and that all mobility scooters were assessed through an independent process to make sure they could be accommodated and taken on and off its vehicles safely.

Magee, who lives in Coleraine, said he bought the new scooter as the previous one had begun to show its age.

He originally contacted the Nolan Show to share his story.

He said he deliberately bought a scooter that was the same size as his old one, thinking it would be suitable to take onto trains, but after it was assessed he got a letter from Translink saying it was too big.

"I felt disheartened, I felt humiliated in so many ways," he said.

"I'm left not being able to go on any trains and I can't use the buses because it will not fit on any of their buses.

"It seems like we're [mobility scooter users] an inconvenience to people.

"I don't like the fact that I use a mobility scooter but unfortunately I've been left with no choice."

News.title: Police to end review into siblings who died in farmhouse 'bloodbath'
News.content:
A forensic review into the deaths of a brother and sister 50 years ago will end almost four years after it began, despite not delivering any new conclusions.

The bodies of Martha and Griff Thomas were found at a farmhouse in Llangolman, Pembrokeshire in 1976, originally prompting a double murder investigation.

Family member Huw Gibby, 79, said he was left "shell-shocked" that the investigation had failed to find any new answers, and described crime scene photos as a "bloodbath".

Dyfed-Powys Police said a "significant amount of complex work" had been undertaken, and "the family has been updated on the limitations faced in reviewing an incident that took place 50 years ago".

On a chilly Saturday morning in December 1976, postman Nigel Rossiter pulled up outside the isolated Ffynon Samson farmhouse in west Wales.

It was his first week in the job, and he spotted a couple of letters still lying on the floor of the porch where he had delivered them days before.

Smelling burning inside, he raised the alarm. This led to the discovery of two bodies, Griff, 73, who was badly burnt, and Martha, 70, who had severe injuries.

Police were called and found Martha, known as Patti, lying slumped on a magazine rack in the corner of the living room, with severe head injuries.

Chairs had been knocked over, and an overturned television lay at her feet. It was still switched on, with the sound of static filling the room.

News.title: Wildfire damage could take hundreds of years to recover from, experts say
News.content:
It could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.

Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.

He expects 2026 to be the worst year Wales has ever experienced.

As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.

In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.

Both fires were visible from space.

Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff.

Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember.

"I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."

While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes.

"If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil.

"So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."

News.title: Veteran camps in woods for months waiting for home
News.content:
An Army veteran has spent the last 15 weeks camping in woods while waiting for his social housing application to be processed.

Blair Murray, 44, served more than a decade in the Royal Logistics Corps up to 2010, but was made homeless by a landlord last year and spent months staying with friends before setting up camp in woodland near Crook in County Durham.

Murray said he had lined up a job and arranged to start counselling sessions, but both were being held up by his lack of a home.

Since the BBC got in touch with Durham County Council, homeless prevention manager Christopher Hepworth said the authority had worked with the Armed Forces Outreach Service and booked him into a hotel.

Hepworth said: "We will continue to work with him to secure suitable, stable, long-term accommodation."

In the most recent survey carried out by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, one in 400 ex-service personnel reported they were homeless or sleeping rough.

News.title: Why is Amanda Knox's upcoming Edinburgh Fringe comedy show causing controversy?
News.content:
Amanda Knox, a woman involved in one of the world's most famous murder cases, is set to perform a comedy show at The Edinburgh Festival Fringe.

Knox was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roommate, Meredith Kercher, in Italy in 2007.

Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain her experiences to her daughter, according to the festival's website.

"I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder," she had told the Telegraph newspaper, external.

Kercher's sister, Stephanie told BBC Breakfast her sibling "wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value".

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women.

A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Find out more about what Stephanie Kercher told the BBC.

Ricky Gervais has addressed viewers who may get offended by his new sitcom Alley Cats, telling them: “You’re an adult.”

The comedian, 65, returned to Netflix with Alley Cats – his first TV comedy since After Life came to an end in 2022 – on Friday (7 August). The animated six-parter sees Gervais and regular collaborators Tom Basden, Andrew Brooke, David Earl and Diane Morgan voice a gang of foul-mouthed, stray felines as they attempt to help a lost kitten get home.

Since its releasem the comedy has received reviews ranging from lukewarm to scathing – with a number of outlets giving it one or two-star ratings. Many critics commented on its excessively sweary and crude dialogue, with The Independent’s Louis Chilton writing in his one-star review: “As TV premises go, ‘Dark Garfield’ is something that might have been transgressive 30 years ago – not today.”

open image in gallery David Earl as Puke, Jo Hartley as Kitten, Diane Morgan as Olive, Ricky Gervias as Gus, Andrew Brooke as Fang, Tom Basden as Ponce in 'Alley Cats' ( PA )

Appearing to acknowledge the criticism, Gervais took to X on Friday morning. “If you watch Alley Cats and you get offended at any point, just remember that 1, It’s just a cartoon about cats, and 2, you’re an adult, and can take it,” he wrote on X, alongside an emoji of a face crying with laughter.

He also reshared The Times’s three-star review, which asked “Is Ricky Gervais’s sweary cat cartoon too much,” writing alongside it: “Hope so.”

As well as in The Independent’s review, which called the show “abrasive, smug, and completely mirthless”, Alleycats was also panned by The Telegraph’s Anita Singh – with the publication saying that it’s “the worst thing to happen to cats since Cats” in a zero-star write-up.

open image in gallery Ricky Gervais returned to Netflix with his first comedy since 'After Life' today ( AFP/Getty )

Metro’s Tom Percival went so far as to say that it is “the worst thing” he’s watched on TV that year and that it is “the televisual equivalent of a black hole of bad ideas”, while The Guardian’s Lucy Mangan wrote that its excellent cast “can’t save it from being lazy, crude and boring”.

After beginning his comedy career in the late Nineties, Gervais shot to stardom with his seminal mockumentary sitcom The Office in 2001. While the show only ran for two series, 15 international versions of The Office have since aired in other countries – with the US show starring Steve Carrell being the longest-running adaptation.

Gervais went on to create the podcast, The Ricky Gervais Show, as well as The Office spin-off film David Brent: Life of the Road, 2009 romcom The Invention of Lying, BBC sitcom Extras and more recently, Netflix’s After Life.

June marked the 25th anniversary of The Office, with stars Makenzie Crook and Martin Freeman taking part in a reunion documentary for the BBC. However, Gervais chose to give it a miss – opting to mark the occasion on his YouTube channel instead with a video looking back on the show’s biggest moments.

Hackers have broken into water systems in at least a dozen states in recent weeks, what cybersecurity experts say should be an urgent wake up call to immense vulnerabilities in American infrastructure.

“Malicious cyber actors” have infiltrated internet-connected water systems that routinely monitor and adjust safe drinking water across the country, according to federal law enforcement agencies.

Officials have not reported any widespread disruptions to America’s drinking water supplies, but analysts who have sounded alarms to governments and utilities for years about national security threats to critical infrastructure say the attacks should spark a nationwide reckoning.

“I’ve spent my 15-year career really trying to avoid being the person that runs around and tries to scare the s*** out of everybody,” Craig Jackson, deputy director of the Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity at the University of California, Berkeley, told The Independent. “That said, I think it’s really, really, really bad, dude.”

President Donald Trump’s own intelligence agencies have suspected Iranian-linked actors were responsible for the latest wave of attacks, but the president has dismissed breaches in Minnesota as the fault of the state’s own government. If the regime is unable to target the U.S. with its own rockets and drones, experts fear the attacks could open a new, asymmetrical front in the administration’s war with Iran.

open image in gallery At least a dozen states have reportedly experienced cyberattacks believed to be launched by Iranian hackers tapping into water treatment systems ( Getty Images )

“I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” the president told reporters at Camp David on July 31 without providing any evidence.

“I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota,” he added. “Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

In a statement on social media, the state’s Governor Tim Walz said that “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too.”

“This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran,” Walz said.

“The reason that we’re not seeing successful attacks at scale against other critical infrastructure in the way that we’re seeing it right now with water — it’s not because all these other sectors are super secure and water is especially vulnerable,” Jackson told The Independent. “It’s because some of our adversaries have decided to screw with our water, because it’s scary.”

open image in gallery The latest breaches include operating technology at more than 30 water systems in the state of Minnesota alone ( AP )

The U.S. is made up of roughly 16,000 wastewater treatment plants and 152,000 public drinking water systems.

That process is controlled by programmable logic controllers, which measure water pressure and chemicals and operate pumps, among other tasks. Hackers appear to have remotely accessed programmable logic controllers that are connected to the internet.

The FBI and Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency have urged utilities to disable internet access, set up strong passwords and revert to manual control, among other changes.

The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition said the attacks deserve more than a handful of alerts from federal agencies. “We must view this through a clear lens: an adversary has directly impacted a core American necessity,” the organization's executive director Tatyana Bolton wrote in an urgent appeal to members of Congress.

Michael Garcia, policy director for the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition, told The Independent that the results of the attacks are the same, regardless of the culprit.

“You have Americans questioning whether or not they could drink their water,” he said. “Hopefully this raises a larger question that our critical infrastructure is vulnerable, and actors will exploit it, and it’s only a matter of time. .. What it comes down to is just actually now taking the action, ensuring that at the local level, these entities are taking the mitigation steps that the government and the manufacturers are suggesting and recommending.”

Experts are very much aware of the obstacles involved in convincing the administration and members of Congress — let alone cash-strapped state and local governments — to invest in sorely needed security updates.

“We’re super, super vulnerable, because the technology — all of our technology — is, generally speaking, built in relatively unsecure ways,” Garcia told The Independent. “And it’s very, very hard in a free market sense to get organizations to invest a lot in reducing this risk.”

Decades of deferred maintenance against growing costs and deteriorating infrastructure have made investments in cybersecurity and operational security measures “a really tough sell,” Jackson said.

open image in gallery Hackers were able to tap into internet-connected programmable logic controllers, which measure water pressure and chemicals and operate pumps, among other tasks, according to federal law enforcement agencies

The Trump administration has also gutted the agency tasked with responding to cybersecurity threats.

The Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency has been villainized by the president and his allies over the agency’s past efforts to disrupt election disinformation and after former director Christopher Krebs publicly assured that the 2020 presidential elections were the “most secure in American history.”

Since taking office, Trump has purged nearly one-third of the agency’s workforce, leaving the agency unprepared to respond to emerging threats from artificial intelligence and a new era of cyberwarfare while the administration is embroiled in a monthslong war with Iran, critics have warned.

Compounding the frustration among national security and cybersecurity experts is that nothing about the latest threats is new.

The attacks are merely the most recent in a string of incidents targeting government agencies, from ongoing phishing and ransomware threats to a malware attack in 2021 that paralyzed the largest fuel pipeline in the U.S.

The long-running Volt Typhoon operation, which the U.S. believes is the work of China’s People's Liberation Army Cyberspace Force, has been accused of hijacking Americans’ internet routers.

The latest attacks are also not the first targeting water systems that have been attributed to Iranian actors. A hacktivist group known as Cyber Av3ngers took credit for a 2023 attack on a Pennsylvania water system that the U.S. has officially attributed to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“I think we have to remember that cyber is just one tool in the tool belt when it comes to geopolitics,” Garcia told The Independent. “Maybe they were trying just to send a shot across the bow, and just do one locality, or just to show the capabilities, but this is a pretty far-reaching campaign that is pretty escalatory and very dangerous.”

A “worst-case scenario” outlook could have led to massive, life-threatening disruptions to the nation’s water system, from cutting off access to water at hospitals and military bases to pumping chemicals into drinking water supplies.

“At the end of the day, I think we were quite lucky that it’s not worse,” Garcia told The Independent. “A worst-case scenario could have been that we didn't catch it.”

President Trump will tell you the grass is always greener. And he means it.

The president frequently touts his knack for creating perfect lawns, bringing up grass in at least 45 public events or interviews over the past 18 months. That is at least once every 12 days.

Trump noted his ongoing enthusiasm for turf as recently as Monday, telling military spouses at a White House event: "Grass is like humans. It has a life."

The commander-in-chief even turned his focus to the plant during an interview with The Spectator just five weeks after his second inauguration.

“You see the grass outside, right?” Trump asked. “Some people would like to leave it. But the problem is, you can’t.”

open image in gallery President Trump has mentioned grass at least 45 times at events and in interviews during his second term ( PA Wire )

The origins of Trump’s love of grass

Trump’s mentions of grass have already far exceeded the 26 times he brought it up during his first four-year term.

However, his love for the plant goes back much further than that.

“I know a lot about grass because I own a lot of golf courses,” he said while announcing the recipients of the Kennedy Center Honors last August. “And, if you don’t have good grass, you’re not in business very long.”

A week later, while visiting park police officers in Washington D.C., the president declared, “I know more about grass than any human being, I think, anywhere in the world.”

Trump’s background as a real estate developer also plays a role in his love for grass, as have his attempts to remake Washington, D.C., in his own image.

Grass has played a big role in Trump’s Washington D.C. makeover

Matt Koch, the lawns research fellow for gardening giant Scotts Miracle-Gro Company, met recently with the president to discuss planting new grass on the White House’s South Lawn.

open image in gallery Trump paved over much of the grass in the White House Rose Garden ( AFP/Getty )

Koch proudly considers himself a “grass nerd” and came away convinced Trump is an honorary one after speaking with him in the Oval Office.

“An amazing dialogue, talking grass for half an hour,” Koch said. “Going back and forth about grass.”

Last September, while hosting Republican lawmakers for dinner, he pledged of green spaces around Washington D.C: “We’re gonna re-grass them with the best guys in the country.”

During an event announcing the intended renaming of the Department of Defense that same month, Trump assured attendees, “I’m very good at grass.”

Trump most frequently mentions grass while touting his efforts to renovate and refurbish landmarks across Washington, D.C.

However, Trump has sometimes expressed frustration with the plant, telling the hosts of the All In podcast during an Oval Office tour: “Problem with the grass, you couldn’t do anything with it.”

open image in gallery Trump often mentions grass while touting his renovations around Washington DC ( Getty )

Trump even mentioned grass while pardoning turkeys

Trump joked about grass while pardoning two turkeys, named Waddle and Gobble, during a Thanksgiving ceremony last year.

“Despite their size, Secretary Kennedy has formally certified that these are the first ever MAHA turkeys,” he said, noting that they had been consuming grass-fed beef.

Trump even mentioned the plant while speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year, pointing again to his D.C. renovations.

“We don't have to worry about fences anymore,” he remarked. “All of the places the grasses are cut and replaced with new grass.”

open image in gallery Trump also said that Marine One has damaged grass surrounding the White House ( AFP/Getty )

Trump added, “In many cases it's all going to happen in the spring. But Washington, D.C., is beautiful again, and it's safe.”

High heels played into his decision to remove much of the White House Rose Garden’s grass

The president has often claimed that women would complain to him about their high heels getting stuck in the mud in the White House Rose Garden.

“The women would be lifting up their shoes, saying, ‘You’ve destroyed my shoes,'” he said last year.

During the White House’s Diwali Festival of Lights event in October 2025, he recalled a state visit from the Prime Minister of India.

“We had the Prime Minister of India here, and they had a lot of press, and the women were walking out with their shoes full of mud,” he said. “So we can't have that.”

When hosting the Los Angeles Dodgers in July, he suggested that women in heels “would go down like quicksand.”

Now, the garden has been paved over and, despite Trump’s love of the plant, contains noticeably less grass.

Trump has wiped out even more grass at the White House

Trump reduced large swaths of the South Lawn to dirt when he ordered a UFC octagon to be erected on the site to mark his 80th birthday celebrations. In the weeks that followed the huge birthday celebration, a sprawling helipad has been built in the octagon’s place.

The construction has removed even more grass from the lawn.

open image in gallery The president is also building a helipad near the White House ( Getty )

However, Trump has said the helipad was needed because the new, more powerful fleet of helicopters now being used as Marine One tore up the previous sod.

“When you land on the grass, it’s not that the grass gets discolored - it gets ripped out,” he said in June.

“Half of the grass was sitting in front of the Oval Office front door,” he said.

Scotts Miracle-Gro donated $1 million in monetary and product support to the National Park Service to restore the South Lawn after the UFC fight. The company's CEO, James Hagedorn, is a Trump supporter.

The president met with Koch in June to select a custom turfgrass blend of four kinds of tall fescues and four Kentucky bluegrasses.

“You can tell he spends a lot of time on golf courses," Koch said. “He obviously owns courses, and he knows grass from being around it.”

Koch returned to the White House last week as crews began resodding some areas of the lawn outside the helipad construction area. There are plans next spring to plant seeds from the grass blend Trump selected.

open image in gallery Donald Trump is a keen golfer, something connected to his love of grass ( PA Archive )

By then, growth will be optimal, and the helipad work should be complete, making the lawn restoration easier.

Trump’s love of grass is connected with his golfing habit

Also key to the president's grass fixation is his love of golf.

Bert McCarty, a Clemson University professor of turfgrass science and management, said golfers appreciate differences in the courses they visit. For example, some beachside spots incorporate the ocean into their course while others use inclines in mountains.

Like most golfers, Trump “likes the challenge of the course and the differences of the course to add variety," McCarty says.

Referencing the home of the Masters tournament last August, Trump vowed that parks in Washington D.C. will “look like Augusta.”

Most people think Augusta is “heaven,” because of its flowers and fairways, McCarty says; however, municipalities often “can’t compete” with the amount spent to achieve that look.

Trump, though, went on to say that D.C. would look like another landmark: “It'll look like, more importantly, Trump National Golf Club. That's even better.”

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Norway's football federation has intensified pressure on Fifa president Gianni Infantino, demanding his immediate resignation following his failed plan to sell World Cup stakes.

Lise Klaveness, president of the Norwegian federation, confirmed her organisation’s stance after a meeting on Thursday, citing a complete loss of confidence.

"We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now," Klaveness told The Guardian. "We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino."

This marks the latest blow for Infantino, with repercussions continuing from his contentious proposal to commercialise World Cup profits via the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

European football's governing body, Uefa, reiterated its threat to boycott the World Cup and other Fifa competitions on Thursday, despite Fifa abandoning the failed scheme. It also reaffirmed its lost confidence in Infantino.

Lise Klaveness has told Infantino there is ‘no way back’ ( Reuters )

Earlier this week, Infantino appeared to have averted an internal revolt during a summit in Rabat, Morocco, with Fifa claiming he received full staff support.

However, Uefa's firm response, swiftly followed by Norway's direct call for his resignation, underscores the enduring anger, particularly in Europe. The English Football Association has also withdrawn its backing for Infantino’s re-election next March, along with the Football Association of Wales (FAW).

Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported that the national federation intends to lodge a new complaint with Fifa's ethics committee. This complaint is expected to encompass the FFE initiative, the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump, and the controversial suspension of Folarin Balogun's World Cup ban.

"We have reached a situation where extraordinary measures are needed to create lasting change," Klaveness asserted.

However, Infantino has received support from other nations as he bids to hold on to his position as Fifa president.

The Confederation of African Football (Caf) voiced its support for Infantino on Thursday, while Mexico and Argentina are also backing the Fifa chief to continue in his role.

Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) called out Infantino for his failed sell-off plan last week, with the proposal eventually scrapped last Friday.

Aldi and Lidl could soon be covered by the same land agreement rules as the UK’s largest supermarket chains.

A proposal by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would prevent the German discount brands from blocking rival supermarkets from opening outlets close to their stores.

The rules designed to stop large grocery retailers from using land agreements to make it harder for rival supermarkets to open nearby, particularly through restrictive covenants and exclusivity arrangements, were first introduced in 2010.

The restrictions currently apply to seven retailers including Asda, Co‑op, Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose.

In a provisional decision, the CMA said it believes Aldi, Lidl GB and Lidl NI should also be subject to the rules.

The regulator said the brands were not originally included in the rules due to their more limited range of products, but said they should now be covered by the restrictions after expanding their shop estate and opening larger stores.

Aldi is the UK’s fourth largest grocer, with a 10.8 per cent share of the market, and Lidl the sixth largest with an 8.8 per cent share, according to recent figures from Worldpanel.

Both Lidl and Aldi have expanded rapidly across the UK in recent years ( PA )

Both companies have rapidly expanded through store openings in recent years, while they have also attracted new shoppers through their discount pricing.

The CMA has said it is seeking further views before reaching a final decision.

Juliette Enser, CMA executive director of competition enforcement and markets, said: “We want everyone to have the best choice of supermarket and range of prices when buying their groceries.

“To ensure this happens, we put rules in place to prevent big supermarket chains blocking rival stores from opening nearby – and now we propose applying those rules to Aldi and Lidl too.

“This is about allowing shoppers to choose where they spend their money and levelling the playing field for all major supermarkets. Today’s proposals are provisional and we welcome views before deciding the best way forward.”

An Aldi spokesperson said: “The CMA’s provisional decision does not impact our long-term growth plans across the UK.

“We remain firmly committed to opening hundreds of new stores across the country, bringing Aldi’s unbeatable value and award-winning quality to even more customers.”

A Lidl spokesman said: “We note the CMA’s provisional decision regarding our status under the Controlled Land Order.

“As a discounter, we have always welcomed and embraced competition within the market and our focus remains on continuing to open new stores and bringing our high-quality, lowest-priced groceries to even more communities. Any outcome will not impact our steadfast momentum and growth.”
