Indian journalist Tarun Tejpal, once among the country’s best-known investigative editors, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after a court convicted him of raping a junior colleague during a work event in 2013.

The Bombay High Court’s Goa bench on Thursday found the 63-year-old founder and former editor-in-chief of investigative news magazine Tehelka guilty of rape and sexual harassment, setting aside a 2021 trial court ruling that had cleared him of all charges.

The judges sentenced him to 10 years’ imprisonment, ordered him to pay fines of around Rs1m (£7,815), with the amount to be paid to the survivor.

Tejpal said he would challenge the ruling in the Supreme Court, and judges granted him four weeks to surrender after his lawyer sought more time to lodge the appeal.

Tejpal, who founded Tehelka in 2000, built a reputation as one of India’s leading investigative journalists through a series of undercover investigations, most notably the “Operation West End” sting into alleged defence corruption.

In November 2013, a junior colleague accused Tejpal of sexually assaulting her twice inside a hotel lift during Tehelka’s annual ThinkFest conference in Goa. The event, attended by politicians, business leaders, and international guests including Robert De Niro, was one of India’s best-known ideas festivals.

The journalist said Tejpal assaulted her on two consecutive days while exploiting his position as her editor. She later resigned from Tehelka, accusing the publication’s leadership of attempting to minimise the allegations and engaging in “tactics of intimidation, character assassination and slander” rather than supporting her, according to her resignation letter to then managing editor Shoma Chaudhury, published in full by India Today.

open image in gallery Indian journalist Tarun Tejpal has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after a court overturned his acquittal and convicted him of raping a junior colleague during a work event ( AFP via Getty Images )

Tejpal was later arrested and spent about seven months in custody before being granted bail by India’s Supreme Court in 2014.

In May 2021, a sessions court in Goa acquitted him of rape, sexual harassment, and other charges, ruling that prosecutors had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The judgment was widely criticised by lawyers, women’s rights campaigners, and legal experts after it questioned the complainant’s conduct after the alleged assaults, saying that she “did not demonstrate any kind of normative behaviour” that a survivor of sexual assault “might plausibly show”.

The judgement also said certain facts created “doubt on the truthfulness of the victim”, and brought up photographs taken shortly after the alleged assaults, saying she was “smiling and looked happy, normal, in good mood”.

The Goa government appealed the acquittal, arguing that the trial court had effectively put the survivor on trial instead of the accused.

In an 81-page judgment delivered on Thursday, the Bombay High Court agreed.

Calling the earlier acquittal “perverse”, Justices Neela Gokhale and Amit Jamsandekar said the trial judge had fallen into the trap of expecting an “ideal” or “perfect” victim and had relied on “stereotypical assumptions” about how a survivor should physically resist or emotionally react after an assault.

The bench also criticised the lower court for allowing the defence to “harass and humiliate” the complainant during cross-examination. The judges described the survivor as a witness of “sterling quality”, held that her testimony did not require independent corroboration to sustain a conviction, and found that CCTV footage and Tejpal’s apology emails supported the prosecution’s case.

open image in gallery Tarun Tejpal is escorted by police officials from a courthouse after being remanded in police custody in Panaji in 2013 ( AFP/Getty )

The judges found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and convicted Tejpal under provisions of the Indian Penal Code covering rape by a person in a position of trust or authority, sexual harassment, and assault with intent to disrobe.

During sentencing, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the Goa government, urged the court to impose the maximum punishment, arguing that Tejpal had abused his position over a woman “of his daughter's age”.

“This court must give out a clear message to society that when a girl says no, it means no,” Mehta told the bench, according to Live Law. “A no means a no.”

Tejpal pleaded for leniency, telling the court: “I am 62 and I believe I am a victim. I have a wife... All that I can say is we can go and appeal. Please be lenient for me.”

Outside court, he said he would challenge the conviction in the Supreme Court and maintained that the prosecution was politically motivated. “For the past 13 years they are after me because of my work with Tehelka,” he told reporters. “There is so much evidence that I should have been acquitted 10 times over.”

The survivor’s mother welcomed the verdict, telling NDTV it had lifted “a heavy weight” after years of legal proceedings. “It was painful long years and took a lot of strength to keep going,” she said.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures. News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

News.title: What I saw in a week on the front line of Afghanistan’s hunger crisis
News.content:
May 15 and 16, 2026

It is the weekend, a small moment to rest, although there is still a lot of work waiting for me. A week in the field does not mean that work in Kabul stops. I try to catch up on my emails and have a planned online interview for an international staff position – since in Europe, Friday is a normal working day. I also review parts of new proposals for donors and our financial planning.

On Saturday, however, I take a short break. Together with the base management team in Helmand, we visit a historical site called Qala-e-Bost, believed to have been built around 3,000 years ago. It is a rare moment to step away from work, followed by lunch with the team.

May 17, 2026

Sunday morning, the first working day of the week, we visit Basrhan Sub Health Centre, run by one of our local partners. As a nurse and former nurse trainer, I feel very much in my element in these health centres. It allows me to engage easily with the team and discuss their work.

I speak with the outreach officer and the vaccinator. They explain that this facility supports 18 outreach locations, each visited at least once a month. They provide vaccinations, raise awareness, and connect communities to the health centre. These visits often take place in simple settings, like mosques.

Immunisation is now well accepted. In the beginning, there was some resistance, but trust has grown over time. Every child is tracked, and if a child misses a vaccination, community health volunteers follow up at home. For extra polio vaccinations, this is carefully recorded by marking a finger of the child – helping ensure that no child is missed. The goal is clear: a polio-free Afghanistan.

I also speak with a mother. She is wearing a burka, so I cannot see her face. She tells me she is 22 years old and holds her 12-month-old son on her lap. She came because he has a fever, but I see a healthy child – something that stands out after my time in the TFU.

She brings her child regularly for follow-up and growth monitoring and the child has never been in a treatment program for malnutrition. She speaks positively about the services. “We are lucky,” she says. “The staff treat us well, and we have access to care in our community.”

Sports.title: Gareth Southgate reveals how he spent World Cup as former England manager says ‘a lot has happened’
Sports.content:
GARETH SOUTHGATE has offered a glimpse into how he spent his first World Cup since resigning as England boss.

The former Three Lions manager, 55, chose to stay out of the public eye during the tournament and rejected punditry roles as he thought it might harm the team’s chances of victory.



England were knocked out in a semi-final defeat by Argentina which opened Southgate’s successor, Thomas Tuchel, up to fierce criticism.

Southgate, who was still on the touchline when England went to the quarter-finals in Qatar four years ago, watched the North American tournament from afar.



Although it wasn’t that far, as part of the Instagram slideshow he posted on Thursday featured snaps from New York.

The pictures were captioned: “A lot has happened over the past couple of months, mixing business with pleasure.

“I’ve had the chance to meet some incredible people, work on some exciting projects, and, most importantly, enjoy some quality downtime with the family. Grateful for it all!”

Southgate’s snaps included him taking in applause from the Royal Box at Wimbledon and posing on the corner of a Manhattan street.

He was also seen giving a motivational talk on stage, enjoying a drink in the exclusive Harvard Club and chatting with Prince William.

It was quite a change of pace from the way Southgate spent some of his summers during eight years in charge of England.

Southgate was linked with a handful of high-profile jobs after stepping down in 2024 following England’s second consecutive defeat in a Euros final.

But he suggested last year that his career as a head coach is probably over.



He told BBC Radio 4: “I’ve had one of the most incredible jobs in football which also had a higher purpose because it was my country.

“That’s going to be very hard to replicate. Having had 37 years in football I’m enjoying finding other areas where I think I might be able to make a difference.”

Sports.title: Man Utd clash against hated rivals free to air on ITV and could see Rashford return for first time in nearly two years

TWO England World Cup stars could make their Manchester United returns on Wednesday in one of the country’s fiercest grudge matches.

The Red Devils’ clash against Leeds could have an additional spark if Marcus Rashford plays his first Man Utd game since 2024.

The England pair have been recuperating for three weeks as per Fifa recommendations after the Three Lions’ third place finish at the World Cup.



If Rashford does appear in the heated fixture – which will be free to air on ITV – it would complete one of the most remarkable homecomings in recent football history.

The 28-year-old last played for Man Utd over 600 days ago.

After making 25 goal contributions for Barcelona last season and repeatedly saying he wanted to remain with the LaLiga champions, Rashford’s future away from Old Trafford seemed certain.

However, the Catalan giants refused to trigger Rashford’s relatively modest £26m release clause, and no other team has been willing to entertain his lucrative wage bill as of yet.

Despite spending the past year and a half out on loan, Rashford remains the Red Devil’s highest earner, netting a lucrative £325k a week.

The England winger’s relationship with his boyhood club blew up in the winter of 2024-25.

Sports.title: Argentina back Gianni Infantino and target being handed World Cup 2030 perk in return
Sports.content:
ARGENTINA have given their backing to Fifa president Gianni Infantino amid rising pressure on his position.

Infantino is under massive scrutiny after his failed bid to sell off chunks of the World Cup.



The Swiss chief wanted to create a subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise, which would have overseen football’s biggest tournament and allowed investors to claim a stake in it.

The proposals were widely condemned by a number of federations, including Uefa – who have threatened a boycott of Fifa tournaments.



They were joined by Concacaf and the AFC, while the English FA and Welsh FA have revoked their support for Infantino.

However, the 56-year-old has had some support, including from Qatar and the Mexican FA, which broke rank with Concacaf to pledge allegiance to him.

And now the Argentine FA have released a statement vowing to stick by Infantino in spite of calls for him to step down.

The federation – who are also hoping to host a full group phase at the 2030 World Cup – admitted Fifa were right to withdraw from their World Cup plan and praised Infantino after he apologised for the debacle.

But they insisted he he had their full backing going forwards.

Their statement read: “On behalf of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), and its Executive Committee, we address you, dear President, and through you to the FIFA board, to express our support for the management carried out during the last 10 years, which had as its main axes the development of football throughout the world and the institutional solidity based on a clear, stable and transparent governance model.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“In this regard, with respect to the recent events that are public knowledge, we must acknowledge the Administration’s decision to withdraw a project that, within the football family and from its inception, generated far more uncertainties than certainties.

“Therefore, it is worth highlighting the acknowledgment of the errors made in that process and the apology expressed in the heartfelt message sent to FIFA’s 211 member associations.

“You are leading a management that has brought about a profound transformation of FIFA; that has opened the doors of the organization to all member associations and confederations, so that through frank and direct dialogue, we can all continue to promote football at all levels and disciplines.”

The AFA went on to say they “believe that the way forward is to continue working under its leadership, in order to continue developing a better and even more inclusive football”.



It comes after Conmebol – which presides over South American football – said it would not back a vote to oust Infantino.

The next World Cup will be co-hosted by Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, alongside main hosts Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

The South American sides are currently due to host one game each, but AFA chief Chiqui Tapia wants Argentina to host an entire group phase – especially if the tournament expands to 64 teams.



He told Diario Ole: “If we start thinking that we are half an hour from Uruguay and an hour and a half from Paraguay and we can do a complete phase in our country.”

Decisions over the World Cup will take a back seat for now as Fifa grapples with the Infantino crisis after holding an emergency meeting in Rabat, Morocco.

Infantino has vowed to fight on after admitting mistakes were made after global outcry over the contentious proposals.

He is likely to face stiff opposition ahead of the Fifa presidential elections on March 18, 2027.

Uefa chief Alexander Ceferin is said to be a candidate, as well as PSG chief Nasser Al-Khelaifi, Arsene Wenger and Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani.

Sports.content:
ARSENAL are reportedly interested in Tottenham captain Cristian Romero – opening the door to a bombshell transfer across North London.

Spurs are still bitter about their star centre-back Sol Campbell leaving them to join the Gunners 25 years on.

Tottenham are expected to sell Romero this summer but an overseas buyer is deemed more likely.

Atletico, meanwhile, have a long-standing interest and are now pursuing him again.

Arsenal are ‘admirers’ of Romero, which Spurs are ‘unaware’ of, but a move between the two clubs is considered a ‘non-starter’.

Romero would provide valuable experience but Cristhian Mosquera, Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Jurrien Timber and Riccardo Calafiori can all step into central defence to cover for Saliba.

Spurs paid £42.5m to sign Romero from Atalanta in 2021, with the defender scoring 13 times in 156 appearances.

Sports.title: Massey-Ellis retires from officiating to take up new role with FA
Sports.content:
Assistant referee Sian Massey-Ellis has retired from officiating and will take up a new role with the Football Association.

Massey-Ellis will become the FA's Senior Manager - Women Referees from September, where she will support and develop female officials across the country and help provide a pathway into the elite game.

The 40-year-old became only the second female assistant referee to officiate in the Premier League when she made her top-flight debut in 2010 and has since worked on more than 150 Premier League matches.

Her career also included five Women's FA Cup finals, while she became the first female assistant referee appointed to the Community Shield. In 2021, Massey-Ellis became the first woman involved in a men's FA Cup final when she served as an assistant VAR, before also working as an AVAR at the 2025 Carabao Cup final.

On the international stage, Massey-Ellis officiated at four Women's European Championships and two Women's World Cups, as well as the 2018 Women's Champions League final. In 2019, she became the first English woman to officiate a men's European fixture when she worked as an assistant referee in the Europa League.

To the young girl who simply loved refereeing, we did it. Thank you, football.

Massey-Ellis, who received an MBE for services to football, said: "Although I am stepping away from the touchline, I am not stepping away from football.

"If my journey has helped change perceptions, open doors or inspire even one young person to believe they belong in the game, then I will consider that one of my greatest achievements.

"As I prepare for one final walk onto the pitch, I leave with nothing but gratitude. It has been the greatest honour to serve the game I love and represent English officiating."

Chief Refereeing Officer Howard Webb described Massey-Ellis as a "powerhouse" whose impact on female officiating "will be felt for years to come".

"Sian has done us proud time and time again - domestically and on the international stage, breaking multiple barriers and setting the standard for those coming through in her footsteps," Webb added.

The teams coming second and third will meet in the eliminator at The Kia Oval on Friday August 14, with the winners of those matches then also making the final.

Net run-rate in The Hundred is the average runs scored by a team over 100 balls in each game minus the average runs scored against them over 100 balls in each game.

Sports.title: Undrafted King leads Panthers to comeback win vs Cardinals in Hall of Fame game
Sports.content:
Undrafted rookie quarterback Haynes King ran in on the final play to give the Carolina Panthers a 33-30 victory over the Arizona Cardinals in the Hall of Fame game that kicked off the NFL preseason on Thursday night.

King, who was the Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year last season at Georgia Tech, was 21 of 34 for 180 yards and two touchdowns. He ran for 39 yards and the winning score.

"Well, that was a lot of fun. Just the back and forth of it. Just a really good game," Panthers coach Dave Canales said.

"The guys were resilient and finish is what we preach as a team. We practice for these situations, end of half, end of game. Haynes did a fantastic job, just keeping the play alive, doing whatever he had to do, run it, throw it. Really proud of the group."

Sports.title: England striker Toney charged with assault
Sports.content:
Ivan Toney, who represented England at this summer's World Cup has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm following a nightclub incident in December 2025; he will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday September 24

England striker Ivan Toney has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm, following a nightclub incident in December 2025.

Toney, who featured at the World Cup and plays his club football for Al Ahli in Saudi Arabia, will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday September 24.

England are due to play World Cup winners Spain two days later in a Nations League game at Wembley.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

The charge relates to an assault which reportedly took place on Wardour Street in London.

Toney was a surprise selection in Thomas Tuchel's England squad this summer and went on to make appearances in the semi-final against Argentina as a late substitute and then started the third-place play-off win over France.

Toney, aged 30, joined Al Ahli in August 2024 from Brentford for a transfer fee of £40m. He scored 72 goals in 141 games for Brentford, including 36 in their three seasons in the Premier League.

Toney missed the first half of the 2023/24 season due to a gambling ban but went on to feature in England's run to the Euro 2024 final. The Saudi Pro League season begins on August 13.

Norrie, who has climbed above Arthur Fery to No 36 in the live rankings will become the new British No 1, but the former Wimbledon semi-finalist has ambitions of collecting the second Masters title of his career with Frenchman Arthur Fils up next.

Sports.title: Mexico and Argentina line up behind Infantino to deepen football’s civil war
Sports.content:
The Mexican football federations have broken ranks with the rest of Concacaf by issuing their public backing for beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino in a move that has deepened world football’s civil war.

Concacaf has called for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance in the light of the World Cup sell-off debacle, and is backing Uefa’s demands for meaningful change, although has yet to follow their European counterparts by threatening to boycott tournaments if they do not achieve their objectives.

A statement issued on Thursday night by the Mexico federation (FMF) went some way towards explaining Concacaf’s reticence, as their second biggest member after the United States was unequivocal in their support for Infantino.

In a Fifa statement released under Infantino’s name on Wednesday, the world governing body had called for its institutional practices to be respected, a coded way of condemning any leadership challenge before next March’s scheduled presidential election, which the FMF endorsed.

“The Mexican Football Federation is convinced that football is its fundamental value and that its best defence lies in institutional integrity and respect for the governance and processes that safeguard it,” the FMF said.

“Therefore, the FMF will not recognise or approve any process convened outside of this institutional framework, and it embraces the call issued by President Infantino on August 5, 2026, to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of its 211 member associations. The FMF supports President Infantino’s leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening.”

The Argentina Football Association (AFA) followed Mexico’s lead by backing Infantino in a gushing tribute and expressing support for his leadership over the past decade.

Unlike Concacaf, South America’s Conmebol appears united behind Infantino, while in an intriguing subplot there is growing speculation that Mexico would like to switch confederations to join the latter.

“In relation to the recent events that are public knowledge, we must recognise the decision of the administration to withdraw a project that generated, within the football family and from its inception, many more uncertainties than certainties,” the AFA statement read.

“That is why it is worth highlighting the acceptance of the errors made in this process and the apology expressed in the heartfelt message displayed to the 211 member associations of Fifa. Prioritising governance standards is a fundamental pillar for strengthening good relations between Fifa, its member associations and the confederations.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“In the same way, and as we have already expressed, you are leading a management that led to a profound transformation of Fifa, which opened the doors of the organisation to all member associations and confederations, so that with a frank and direct dialogue, we can, together, continue to promote football at all levels and disciplines.

“From our point of view, this transformation was based on a model of transparent governance, respect for statutory structures and the monitoring of democratic procedures, essential principles for the football family to be united, firm and working to continue generating improvements in sports and institutions, which have an impact on a better quality of life for millions of human beings who practice our beloved sport.

“Accordingly, with the upcoming Fifa Congress approaching, the association that we proudly preside over firmly believes and reaffirms that the way forward is to continue to work under your leadership, so that we can continue to develop better and even more inclusive football.”

Earlier on Thursday the Confederation of African Football had reaffirmed its support for Infantino, providing him with further allies as he fights to extend his 10-year reign.

Sports.title: Norway’s Klaveness tells Fifa president Infantino to resign: ‘There is no trust now’
Sports.content:
The Norwegian FA will ask Gianni Infantino to resign with immediate effect after his doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Norway is the first federation to call directly for the Fifa president to step down after a series of controversies that came to a head with the current crisis surrounding his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme.

The decision was made at a meeting of the Norwegian Football Federation board (NFF) on Thursday night. Norway has consistently taken a lead in efforts to scrutinise Fifa’s governance and recent events have taken any faith in its leadership beyond the point of no return.

“We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now,” the NFF president, Lise Klaveness, told the Guardian. “We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”

The NFF is expected to formally write a letter requesting Infantino’s resignation in the coming week. Norway was among a handful of countries not to back his re-election as president next March, although several European federations have withdrawn their endorsement in the past week.

“We understand that we’re one country, but it’s our position,” Klaveness said. “It’s just one step further for us. We did not vote for him in 2023 but we hoped we would support him, he was elected and the reason why we were so clear in our statements was to really give the signal that we wanted him to implement the good reforms he was part of. But he didn’t, and now we will ask him to resign.”

Norway will also formalise a fresh complaint to Fifa’s ethics committee on three fronts, taking in the FFE scandal, the award of Fifa’s “peace prize” to Donald Trump and the Folarin Balogun affair of the recent World Cup. It will attempt to bring a number of major federations onboard for its submission.

Sports.title: Tottenham and Atlético in talks over Romero with Van de Ven set to sign new deal
Sports.content:
Tottenham are in talks with Atlético Madrid over the sale of Cristian Romero after categorically rejecting Arsenal’s approach for the Argentina defender and are expected to agree a new five-year deal with Micky van de Ven.

Romero has made no secret of his desire to leave Spurs despite signing a new four-year contract at the start of last season and had looked set to join Internazionale for a fee of around £35m. But Atlético are long-term suitors of the 27-year-old and are thought to be his preferred destination, with Diego Simeone’s side understood to be prepared to match Inter’s bid.

Reports in Spain on Friday suggested that personal terms have already been agreed with Romero, although his move may have to wait for Atlético to free up space in their squad before they can complete the transfer. Nahuel Molina, Romero’s Argentina teammate, is expected to join Roma while Aston Villa are hoping to sign Matteo Ruggeri.

Arsenal had also made their interest known as they search for a replacement for William Saliba, with the Frenchman out for an extended period due to a back issue. But Tottenham – who have signed defenders Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi this summer – insisted that they did not want to sell to another Premier League club, least of all their north London rivals. Arsenal are also interested in Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa.

It is understood that Van de Ven had been considering his future in north London at the start of the summer after Tottenham narrowly avoided relegation last season. But the impact of the new manager, Roberto De Zerbi, has persuaded the Netherlands international to commit his future to the club after talks with his representatives.

Tottenham have already spent more than £200m on six new players this summer and are still in the market for a new attacker. Last week, De Zerbi said that they had “completed 60% of our project in the transfer market”.

Sports.title: England striker Ivan Toney charged with assault after Soho nightclub incident
Sports.content:
The England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault after an incident at a nightclub in Soho in December last year.

Scotland Yard said the striker had been charged on 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 24 September.

The Sun newspaper reported in December that Toney had been arrested after an alleged headbutt. It claimed a fan recognised the footballer and grabbed at him while seeking a photograph with him prior to the incident.

On Friday the Metropolitan police said the charges related to an incident on 6 December at a nightclub on Wardour Street in central London, reportedly the now-closed 100 Wardour Street.

A spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney was at the centre of one of the most curious transfers on deadline day in August 2024 when he completed a late move from Brentford to Al-Ahli worth a reported £40m. He has also played for Newcastle United and his hometown club Northampton Town, as well as several others on loan as he looked to establish himself.

Seen as a late bloomer in football terms, he had made only two Premier League appearances before his 25th birthday, but went on to score 67 goals in 128 appearances over the next three seasons at the top level.

He has played 10 times for England, scoring once in a friendly match against Belgium in 2024, and was part of the 2026 World Cup squad, making appearances against Argentina in the semi-final and in the win over France as England finished third.

Sports.title: Afcon’s biennial switch cost African governing body deal worth more than $1bn
Sports.content:
A deal worth at least $1bn in secured income over eight years was abandoned by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) because the governing body decided to switch the Africa Cup of Nations from a biennial to a four-yearly event, the Guardian can reveal.

On 5 July 2025, the eve of the delayed Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, the Caf president, Patrice Motsepe, told the Guardian in Rabat, after a prolonged discussion of the bidding process at an executive committee meeting, that a decision on a winning bid would be made “in due course”.

“We announced in Addis Ababa this $1bn partnership that we are looking at over the next eight years. There is a lot of good progress that has been made,” he said.

On 23 July, four days after the World Cup final in New York, Caf opened a fresh tender for the marketing and commercial rights of the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) tournaments, with bidders given until 24 August to hand in their bid books.

The tender is in complete contrast to the 2025 bidding round, in which the entirety of Caf’s competition portfolio was bundled for sale.

Luxolo September, Caf’s head of communications, confirmed that the change in Afcon frequency is wholly responsible for the abandonment of the 2025 bidding round that was on the verge of completion.

“As foreshadowed by the president in his comments last year, following the receipt and evaluation of bids and presentations from the bidders, in the second half of 2025, Caf entered into detailed discussions with shortlisted bidders regarding the precise terms and conditions of their proposals.

“However, at its meeting on 20 December 2025, the Caf executive committee took a unanimous decision – in the interest of African football – to move the Afcon to a four-year cycle, bringing the competition into alignment with the international match calendar,” September said. “This was a significant decision for African football. That executive committee decision materially changed the scope of the commercial rights available for tender, with the result that the 2025 ITT (Invitation To Tender) process could no longer proceed in its existing form.”

View image in fullscreen Patrice Motsepe (left) said in 2025 that ‘good progress’ was being made over a $1bn deal for Caf. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

It has been seven years since Caf has had a long-term deal to secure its financial future. The 2016-2028 billion-dollar “minimum guarantee” revenue contract that it signed with the French company Lagardère during the tenure of Issa Hayatou, the late Cameroonian president of Caf, was the first of its kind for the organisation.

“The Memorandum of Understanding with Lagardère was agreed by a team I led with Hicham [El Amrani, then Caf general secretary] in May 2015, in Zurich,” Suketu Patel, then chair of Caf’s finance committee, said in 2019.

“On that same day, we met with Infront. Their indicative offer on the table was a $450m minimum guarantee for eight years, as opposed to the $1bn, for 12 years, from Lagardère.

“If you look at our earlier contract of 2009, we had a minimum guarantee of $150m, but our income for the period was actually around $350m. We anticipated that the 12-year contract would have yielded about $1.3bn.

“I can tell you that whilst President Hayatou and I had differences on political matters, we never had one on the management of Caf finances. He did not interfere with the processes established for good governance.”

But that agreement was unilaterally terminated in December 2019 during the tenure of Ahmad Ahmad, Hayatou’s successor as Caf president.

A protracted legal dispute at the International Chamber of Commerce led to Caf, just over a year into the presidency of Motsepe, paying Lagardère a final settlement of $50m, as compensation for the breach of contract, just before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“There is no way that any sponsor will be prepared to pay the same amount of money for a deal in which you would normally have four Afcons over an eight-year period, when you will now only have two. That is certainly a no-brainer,” said a former FA president with expertise in financial matters.

Sports.title: Behind Milburn’s magic: Wor Jackie was a pit village hero and ‘everybody’s friend’ in Newcastle
Sports.content:
Of all the footballers who have worn the black and white, that possessive geordie pronoun “Wor” (our) was unique to Jackie Milburn; for he was a man of the people as much as he was a great sportsman. In that respect, his birthplace of Ashington in Northumberland only added to the mythology.

“The biggest pit village in the world,” as it was known, was the north-east in microcosm – a one-horse coal town where miles of identical terraced houses spread out from the pitheads and the menfolk were obsessed by whippets, leeks, association football and pints in the club. Nevertheless, he had a self-discipline that saw the pitfalls of alcohol: “Certainly it prevented my dad, Alec Milburn, from making the big time,” Jackie recalled. “He could have gone to Tottenham but preferred to stay home and drink his ale.”

At the St James’ Park homecoming following the 1951 FA Cup final, “Wor Jackie” (by which epithet his skipper Joe Harvey introduced him) was invited to address the throng. “At first I tried to ‘talk posh,” Jackie later recalled, “then there was a roar of laughter when a voice shouted, ‘Taak tiv us in your own language, Jackie!’” The dialect of Ashington is one of the most melodious varieties of the ‘pitmatic’ geordie of the coalfields, and still the butt of numerous jokes to this day (when an electrician asked a barmaid where the mains were, the answer came, “Tha just doon there, past the ladies.”)

View image in fullscreen A statue by Tom Maley of Jackie Milburn at Woodhorn Colliery Museum, near Ashington in Northumberland. Photograph: John Angerson/Alamy

Jackie’s lineage was important, for Ashington was an unusually fertile footballing hotbed. His great-grandfather, “Warhorse” Milburn, had kept goal for Northumberland in the 1880s, and young Jackie grew up reading about the Football League exploits of his four Milburn cousins who played professionally, while another cousin, Cissie Charlton, née Milburn, was later almost equally famous as the mother of World Cup winners Jack and Bobby.

Although the coalmines of Ashington demanded their human tribute, professional football was a feasible way out for many – and Milburn once counted 47 local boys he knew of who had played in the First Division. In his 1957 autobiography Golden Goals, he recalled waking early one Christmas morning to find a new pair of football boots at the end of the bed. He slipped them on straight away and headed out into the back lane at half past three in the morning only to find “most of my friends, wearing their new boots, playing football by torchlight in the middle of the street”.

View image in fullscreen Jackie Milburn’s second cousin Bobby Charlton thought that ‘his ball control at speed was as good as anyone I’ve seen’. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

The prevailing work ethic in pit villages throughout the coalfield helped to mould such formidable players. Miners were famed for their stamina, and with generations of pitmen in his family tree Milburn’s genetics shaped the way he played. In Ashington folklore it was told that Jackie kicked the same stone to school and back for three years, and his one-time teammate Len Shackleton was always impressed by his tenacity and “never-say-die spirit”. This was exemplified by tireless high pressing, and a trademark sliding tackle that hooked the ball from any defender unwise enough to prevaricate on the ball. In his early life he had made money as a sprinter, competing at Edinburgh in the famous Powderhall Handicap and running 100 yards in around 10 seconds.

With his pace, allied to phenomenal shooting power with either foot Milburn rightly takes his place in the Newcastle pantheon. His record of 200 goals in 401 appearances is second only to that of Alan Shearer.

Until 1948 Milburn combined football with work at local collieries, and as he didn’t then have a car, with almost too-perfect symbolism he would take the bus from Ashington into Newcastle with the same supporters who would pay to watch him. “The size of the crowd meant that it sometimes took us up to three-quarters of an hour to walk up the bank and round to the players’ entrance,” Milburn recalled. “But what could we do? Our supporters were a marvellous warm-hearted lot. They even flooded the club with clothing coupons to help kit out the side.” That cosy, close-knit and deeply sociable world of the postwar north-east suited Jackie down to the ground.

View image in fullscreen Newcastle United captain Joe Harvey (c) introduces Prime Minister Winston Churchill (l) to Jackie Milburn (r) before the 1952 FA Cup final. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

“He was everybody’s friend!” wrote his famous second cousin Jack Charlton. “If you ever walked through Newcastle with him, you got stopped every two minutes; everybody said hello to him.”

Yet he never sought this fame, and it’s telling that whenever he went to the pictures in Ashington, he always waited until the lights were down before he entered the auditorium. Here was a modest and even shy man, who shared the small-c conservatism that characterised the otherwise Labour-voting north-east. He was thrilled to meet Winston Churchill at Wembley in 1952 – “the greatest hero of my life whose bust has occupied pride of place in our house since 1948” – as well as the ailing King George VI, whose courage he admired.

View image in fullscreen Newcastle centre forward Jackie Milburn with his wife Laura and daughters Linda (3) and Betty (2) in front of a picture on the wall of Milburn shaking hands with King George VI at the 1951 Cup Final, when his goal won the Cup for Newcastle. Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images

In Golden Goals Milburn presents an image to the world of domestic bliss with his wife, Laura, admitting his aversion to gardening and patterned socks, and his enjoyment of watching TV, reading thrillers and going to the dog track most Wednesdays (greyhounds were always a miners’ passion).

Due to the dominance of a handful of dangerous, heavy industries it was a truism to say that communities across the north-east thrived on being in it together. This may have been one of the reasons why Jackie never quite made a consistent mark on the international stage, despite his 13 caps and 10 goals for England. In later life he confessed that many of his international teammates were too self-obsessed to play as a team and even suggested that “one or two of them were outright snobs”.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester City defenders can only stop and stare as Newcastle United’s Jackie Milburn (left) heads home to score his first-minute goal in the 1955 FA Cup final. Photograph: Popperfoto/Getty Images

Milburn became talismanic for Newcastle. When United’s new manager Dugald Livingstone took the probably rational decision to drop the ageing Milburn for the 1955 FA Cup final against Manchester City on form and fitness grounds, the wily former manager Stan Seymour – by then back upstairs in the boardroom – stepped in to overrule him. Milburn was duly reinstated and would score what was then the fastest Cup final goal – with a rare bullet header from a corner after only 45 seconds.

The people of the area saw in Jackie Milburn the image of their favourite son. He was modest, witty, warm and honest. He was effortlessly, unaffectedly dashing and handsome. He was hard when necessary, but always ready with a grin and a conciliatory word. He was a canny lad with a passion for his homeland.

He was never cautioned in his 14-year career, and the noted First Division whistler Arthur Ellis concluded that: “If there were 22 players on the field like Jackie you wouldn’t need a referee!” His teammate Joe Harvey noted that Jackie was “gentle and generous in victory, always first with the handshake in defeat”, and Milburn himself conceded that his innate courtesy, and tendency to play in colleagues when he had a chance to shoot himself, was a drawback. “I had a lack of devil.”

It’s amazing to think how much more lethal a ruthless Jackie Milburn would have been. But then he probably wouldn’t have been so endearing.

Sports.title: Arsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032
Sports.content:
Vinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid. Arsenal had been heavily linked with a move for the Brazil international, who had entered the final 12 months of his deal at the Bernabéu.

A tumultuous 2025-26 campaign in which Real failed to win a trophy and initial uncertainty after the arrival of José Mourinho in Madrid alerted the Premier League champions, but Vinícius has now committed his long-term future to the Spanish club.

“Real Madrid and Vinícius Júnior have agreed on the extension of our player’s contract, which links him to the club until 30 June 2032,” a club statement read.

“Vinícius Júnior joined Real Madrid in July 2018 at the age of 18. In his eight seasons wearing our jersey, he has played 375 matches, scored 128 goals, and won 14 titles: two Champions Leagues, three Club World Cups, two Uefa Super Cups, three La Liga titles, one Copa del Rey, and three Spanish Super Cups.

“His contribution to all these titles has been pivotal due to his gameplay, assists, and goals.”

Vinícius wrote on Instagram: “Eight years at the Bernabéu are too few … six more years, and for ever!”

The 26-year-old had hinted at extending his association with Real during an in-house interview on Tuesday where he spoke about Mourinho wanting him to be “happy” and “joyful” after a difficult spell.

A shock last-16 World Cup exit in America with Brazil also added to a frustrating 12-month period for Vinícius, but with his future settled the former Flamengo prospect will aim to help Real get back to competing for major honours again under Mourinho.

Sports.title: Kerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switch
Sports.content:
The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report back for pre-season training at Manchester City in July before her transfer to Barcelona had been agreed.

Barcelona announced their signing of the 26-year-old on Tuesday but it was not until Thursday evening when Manchester City first made any reference to the transfer, eventually confirming they had received a WSL record fee for a sale more than 48 hours later.

Several staff and players at Manchester City were disappointed at what were perceived to be efforts by Kerolin to force a transfer to Barcelona and that her time at the club ended on a surprisingly sour note. She did not join pre-season with the Women’s Super League champions, which began in late July, despite previously having been felt to have been on good terms with the squad.

The deal, worth an initial €1.2m (£1m), represents the largest transfer fee received by a WSL club, and it could rise with add-ons to approximately £1.25m, although this has not been officially confirmed. It is one of the largest transfer fees in women’s football.

City said of Kerolin: “She grabbed 14 goals and six assists during that time, helping City to a WSL and FA Cup double in her solitary full season in England. And upon her transfer to Barça, City have received a WSL-club record transfer fee of €1.2m.

“Everyone at Manchester City would like to thank Kerolin for all her efforts at the club and wish her the very best in her future career.”

Kerolin was part of the City side that lifted their first WSL title in a decade last season and also helped them win the Women’s FA Cup. But within weeks of those celebrations many of her City colleagues have been stunned after she did not say goodbye in-person. Kerolin’s representatives have been contacted for a response.

High-profile examples of such transfer standoffs have been seen in men’s football, but incidents in the women’s game have been comparatively rare.
