World.title: Four Estonians officiated at UEFA's Thursday matches
World.content:
Estonian football officials were active across several UEFA Europa League and Conference League football matches on Thursday, serving as both delegates and referee observers.

Sergei Hohlov-Simson was UEFA delegate for the second-tier Europa League third-round qualifier clash between Kuopio Palloseura of Finland and Romania's Craiova Universitatea. Kuopio reached the stage after losing in the Champions League second qualifying round to Azerbaijan's Sabah Baku. The Romanian had, meanwhile, narrowly lost at the same stage to Bulgaria's Levski Sofia. Thursday's encounter finished 1-1.

Hannes Kaasik headed to Ireland to be a referee observer at Danish club Midtjylland's 2-0 win over Ireland Men's Premier Division Bohemian F.C. at the Tallaght Stadium in Dublin. The match was a UEFA Conference League third-round qualifier, first leg. Midtjylland had previously dropped down from the Europa League after losing to Turkey's Besiktas.

Meanwhile Uno Tutk was referee observer for Hapoel Tel Aviv's 2-0 home win over Polish side GKS Katowice, in the same competition.

Also in the Conference League, Siim Juks was the delegate for Hajduk Split's (Croatia) first leg 5-2 win away to Žalgiris (Lithuania). The latter had previously come back from a 3-0 deficit away to win 7-2 at home against Dinamo Tbilisi to make it to the third round. Hajduk had moved in the opposite direction, dropping down from the Europa League after losing in extra time to Cyprus's Pafos in the second qualifying round.

Two Estonian teams took part in Conference League matches as well, though both were defeated: Paide Linnameeskond lost 4-1 at home to big-name visitors Rapid Vienna in Tallinn, while Tallinna F.C. Flora were beaten 2-0 away to Andorran league champions.

World.title: Authorities issue permit to hunt two bears that entered home yards
World.content:
The Environmental Board on Thursday issued special permits to hunt two bears born last year in the Võõbu village area of Järva County. The animals continued entering home yards despite repeated attempts to scare them back into the forest.

The animals are about a year and a half old and show no fear of people, which means they could pose a danger, the Environmental Board said.

Tanel Türna, head of the hunting and aquatic wildlife department at the Environmental Board, said the young bears' behavior has been extremely unusual.

"Yesterday the bears were in people's yards in Võõbu village in Järva County and did not even fear a rescue truck's siren. Unfortunately, it cannot be ruled out that people themselves caused this behavior — bears of this age should have learned to avoid humans, not look for food in settlements. Based on what we know, it seems people have fed them and disrupted their natural behavior. All usual deterrent methods have been tried repeatedly, but the animals have consistently returned to settlements, which shows a developed behavior pattern," Türna said.

Three bears have actually been seen in the area, but one has not returned to settlements as often.

Türna said nuisance‑bear permits are not issued lightly and are a last resort.

"We have spoken with zoos and wildlife parks — they cannot take the bears into their collections. The Environmental Board understands and appreciates people's desire to help wild animals in trouble. Still, we ask people not to seek contact with wild animals and certainly not to feed them. Otherwise, they may lose their fear of humans and their ability to survive independently — which is exactly what has happened now, and bears that keep returning to settlements may pose a danger to pets and people," Türna said.

The Climate Ministry changed hunting rules in April so bears may only be hunted with a special permit from the Environmental Board. The permit‑based approach allows more flexible solutions to ongoing predator conflicts by directing hunting to areas with damage and at biologically suitable times, the Environmental Board said.

There is no longer a bear hunting season with fixed start and end dates. The Environmental Board may issue permits year‑round if the decision is thoroughly considered. A permit may be issued only to prevent repeated bear damage and dangerous situations. Including Thursday's permits, the Environmental Board has issued six bear‑hunting permits this year.

The brown bear population has been growing since 2013 and is currently estimated at about 1,100 in Estonia.

Bears are increasingly seen in settlements and nearby areas, often drawn by easily accessible food.

"People must be careful and prevent easy access to food that attracts bears. They must not be fed. We ask that leftover garden produce be stored in closed compost bins or sealed compost containers," the Environmental Board said.

Marko Vinni Autor/allikas: ERR

Hunters' Society estimates 1,500 bears in Estonia.

"Right now the situation is such that traditional bear hunting can practically no longer be carried out," said Estonian Hunters' Society adviser Marko Vinni. "Naturally this increases the bear population every year, the number of bears grows and at some point it may exceed society's tolerance."

According to the Environmental Agency, 300 bear cubs are born in Estonia each year, and even accounting for natural mortality, as many as 200 bears may be added to the wild annually, Vinni said. Hunters estimate that 1,500 bears currently live in Estonia. "I think that is not an exaggeration."

Vinni said that because the first special permits for bear hunting were issued only two weeks ago, no bears have been hunted yet in Estonia this year. "I think that of the [traditional] 150 bears, we will not hunt even ten by the end of the year."

Vinni noted that bear meat is a delicacy and restaurants would very much like to have it. "In that sense it has a very practical use, just like other game species."

World.title: Rait Kallus: Is Estonia planning future traffic based on the past?
World.content:
If autonomous vehicles become widespread at the pace currently forecast, today's decisions in city planning may prove inadequate within just a few decades, writes Rait Kallus.

The world is on the brink of the biggest transformation in transportation since the invention of the internal combustion engine. Self-driving cars are no longer the stuff of science fiction but a rapidly advancing technology whose impact on cities may be greater than we can currently imagine.

According to forecasts generated by various artificial intelligence models and transportation analyses, the widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could increase traffic volumes on city streets by roughly 30 to 50 percent. If that scenario materializes, a four-lane road may no longer be sufficient in the future, with capacity needing to expand to the equivalent of six lanes. Likewise, a major highway that now has three lanes in each direction may eventually require five lanes in each direction.

The reasons are straightforward. A self-driving car no longer has to wait in a parking lot or driveway. It can drive to pick up its owner, take the children to school, then head to pick up another family member or travel on its own to its next assignment. Every such empty trip adds more vehicle miles traveled. Even if the total number of cars does not increase significantly, the burden on city streets could grow substantially.

The largest share of public transit users consists of people who rely on it out of necessity rather than preference, such as young people who do not yet have a driver's license. This group stands to benefit the most from autonomous vehicles, since they would be able to travel independently and safely without a license. It is reasonable to assume that a large share of them — estimated at more than 70 percent — would choose personal transportation over public transit under those circumstances.

Another major user group consists of older adults, for whom convenient door-to-door travel is the highest priority. If autonomous transportation becomes significantly cheaper than taxi service, a substantial share of this group as well — estimated at 50 to 60 percent — could prefer self-driving vehicles to conventional public transit.

If these developments occur, public transit in Estonia could lose more than half of its current ridership. That would fundamentally alter the traffic models and assumptions on which cities and transportation infrastructure are currently planned.

Unfortunately, urban planning in Estonia is often moving in the opposite direction. Instead of preparing for future traffic volumes, many places are reducing the capacity available for automobile traffic. If autonomous vehicles become widespread at the pace currently forecast, today's decisions could prove inadequate within just a few decades.

If traffic volumes increase to the extent projected by multiple forecasts, rebuilding individual intersections or optimizing traffic signal timing will no longer be enough.

Self-driving Tesla vehicle. Source: ERR

Tallinn needs strong transportation arteries — fast primary connections that function like the arteries of the human body. The heart could not supply the body if its arteries were replaced with veins, and the same principle applies to urban traffic. If the main transportation corridors become slow, fragmented or too limited in capacity, the city itself begins to suffer and decline.

Whether these transportation arteries follow existing major roads, pass through neighborhoods or are built partly along new routes is ultimately a matter of planning. What matters is that they provide enough capacity to meet future transportation needs.

At the same time, not every mode of transportation has to share the same street space. Pedestrians, cyclists and green spaces also need uninterrupted networks of their own, which do not have to run alongside roadways. When every mode of transportation is given space suited to its purpose, mobility, safety and the overall quality of the urban environment all improve simultaneously.

Urban planning and street network design are investments that last at least half a century. New buildings are designed with a 50-year service life, but they often remain in use much longer. The same is true of streets, intersections, bridges and the urban environment as a whole. That means every decision made today will shape how people move around cities well into the middle of the next century.

If we design cities around yesterday's traffic model, we may discover that the infrastructure we build no longer meets society's actual needs. The purpose of urban planning is not to react to change after the fact, but to anticipate it.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate continues to rise in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar compared to the Iraqi dinar rose on Thursday in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, and the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Erbil.

The US dollar exchange rate slightly rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,523.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,520.5 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,530 Iraqi dinars and 1,520 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also rose, fluctuating between 1,525.5 and 1,525 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq to increase production from Kirkuk oil fields
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair announced on Thursday plans to increase oil production from the Kirkuk oilfields.

The decision intends to capitalize on a recent agreement with Turkey for exporting oil to the port of Ceyhan.

This move also aims to circumvent the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and increase Iraq’s oil exports via ports on the Mediterranean.

The instruction utilizes the recently expanded Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline deal, with the goal of increasing exports from 180,000 barrels per day to approximately 750,000 barrels per day.

Khudair stated that increasing production lays the groundwork for boosting export volumes through Turkey to 1.5 million barrels per day.

Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) has officially partnered with British Petroleum (BP) to bolster cooperation in oil and natural gas projects in Kirkuk oilfields.

In 2025, BP reached a deal with Iraq’s North Oil Company (NOC) to develop oil fields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk, with investments projected to reach $25 billion.

The step is part of the Iraqi government’s attempts to optimize energy sector investments, increase oil output, and minimize gas flaring.

The enhanced output directly addresses the Iraqi government’s growing deficit as a result of continued maritime restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

By producing more petroleum from Kirkuk, Baghdad reduces internal shipping expenses from southern fields while increasing supplies to global markets via outlets on the Mediterranean.

World.title: Iraqi Prime Minister orders higher military readiness as security tensions rise
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ali Al-Zaidi has directed all security and military formations to raise their operational readiness and combat preparedness, according to the Security Media Cell.

The directive aims to maintain a high state of preparedness across Iraq’s security forces through intensified training exercises and operational movements designed to strengthen national security and protect public interests.

In a statement, the Security Media Cell said the Commander-in-Chief instructed security and military forces to increase their level of readiness while conducting training exercises and field movements.

The measures are intended to ensure that all security formations remain fully prepared to carry out their assigned duties and respond to potential security developments.

According to the statement, the directive is part of ongoing efforts to maintain continuous operational readiness across Iraq’s armed forces.

The Security Media Cell said the enhanced readiness program is designed to reinforce Iraq’s security framework and improve the capabilities of military and security units.

Officials stated that maintaining high readiness contributes to:

Strengthening national security.

Preserving public stability.

Protecting Iraqi citizens.

Safeguarding public institutions and national interests.

The government has increasingly emphasized preparedness amid evolving regional security challenges.

The announcement comes during a period of elevated security concerns in Iraq following recent regional developments and heightened tensions involving armed groups.

The official statement, however, does not specify any particular threat or military operation linked to the readiness order.

Some media reports and political analysts have suggested the move may be connected to broader security developments or precautionary planning ahead of upcoming government deadlines. These assessments are analytical interpretations and were not included in the official Security Media Cell statement.

The latest directive reflects Baghdad’s continued focus on ensuring the operational effectiveness of Iraq’s security institutions.

By ordering additional training activities and maintaining high alert levels, the government aims to preserve stability while ensuring security forces remain prepared to respond to any developments affecting the country’s security environment.

World.title: Iraqi Drilling Company completes well rehabilitation at West Qurna 1 oil field
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Drilling Company (IDC) has successfully completed the rehabilitation of oil well WQ1-132 at the West Qurna 1 oil field, marking another step in Iraq’s efforts to enhance oil production efficiency and support the long-term development of its energy sector.

The project was carried out as part of the company’s operational program to improve well performance and maintain sustainable crude oil production.

According to a statement issued by the Iraqi Drilling Company, the rehabilitation work was completed in line with directives from Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi and under the supervision of the company’s Director General, Mohammed Hantoosh Asad Al-Azirjawi.

Technical and engineering teams carried out the operation using the company’s specialized expertise and equipment.

The company said the rehabilitation project forms part of its broader strategy to improve the efficiency of existing oil wells while supporting sustainable production across Iraq’s major oil fields.

Restoration work on producing wells helps maximize output, extend operational life, and improve field performance without the need for entirely new drilling operations.

The Iraqi Drilling Company emphasized that the successful completion of the project reflects the capabilities of its engineering and technical staff, who continue to execute specialized rehabilitation operations according to approved operational plans.

The company noted that relying on local expertise strengthens operational efficiency while supporting the continued development of Iraq’s oil infrastructure.

West Qurna 1 is one of Iraq’s largest producing oil fields and plays a significant role in the country’s crude oil output.

Ongoing rehabilitation and maintenance projects are designed to ensure production stability, improve operational reliability, and meet the technical requirements of field development programs.

The completion of well WQ1-132 is expected to contribute to maintaining efficient production operations within the field as Iraq continues investing in the modernization of its energy sector.

World.title: Iraqi PM, Kurdistan president discuss Erbil-Baghdad cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and the president of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Nechirvan Barzani, discussed on Wednesday the country’s political, economic, and security situation.

During their meeting in Baghdad, the two leaders indicated that it is important to boost cooperation between the federal government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to enhance stability, address challenges, and serve the interests of the Iraqi people, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

Al-Zaidi affirmed the government’s commitment to resolving outstanding issues in line with the constitution, preserving Iraq’s unity, and strengthening national partnership.

Barzani stated that it is important to continue dialogue between national parties. He added that the KRG supports the federal government’s efforts to enhance stability and promote national development.

The discussions focused on approaches to secure the success of the government’s national agenda.

This high-level meeting comes after al-Zaidi’s trips to Turkey and Iran, where he met top officials, and Barzani’s visit to Damascus, where he met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

World.title: Iraq wins legal case in Jordan for Samarra Pharmaceutical Company
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Justice has announced a legal victory before the Jordanian judiciary after securing a final court ruling in favor of the State Company for Drug Industries and Medical Appliances in Samarra, a subsidiary of the Ministry of Industry and Minerals.

The ruling requires a Jordanian company to pay financial compensation following a dispute over the supply of medical materials that failed to meet agreed specifications.

According to a statement from the Ministry of Justice, the ministry’s Legal Department successfully represented the Iraqi pharmaceutical company throughout all stages of the legal proceedings before Jordanian courts.

The case involved a supply contract under which the Jordanian company was expected to provide metal covers for medical supplies. However, the supplier allegedly delivered products that did not comply with the contractual specifications.

Director of the Legal Department, Haitham Mohi Radi, said the final judgment issued by the Jordanian Court of Cassation, and upheld by both the Court of Appeal and the Court of First Instance, ordered the Jordanian company to pay financial amounts to the Samarra-based pharmaceutical company.

The ruling concludes a lengthy legal process aimed at protecting the contractual rights of the Iraqi state-owned enterprise.

The Ministry of Justice described the outcome as an important achievement in safeguarding Iraq’s financial interests abroad.

Officials said the successful litigation reflects the ministry’s continued efforts to defend state institutions before international courts and judicial authorities while protecting public funds from contractual violations.

The ministry added that the case demonstrates the expertise and professionalism of Iraq’s legal teams in handling international commercial disputes.

By successfully pursuing the claim through multiple judicial levels in Jordan, the Legal Department reinforced Iraq’s commitment to enforcing contractual rights and ensuring accountability in cross-border commercial agreements.

The decision is expected to strengthen confidence in the government’s ability to defend the interests of Iraqi public institutions through legal channels.

World.title: Ammar Al-Hakim and Iranian Science Minister discuss academic cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The head of Iraq’s National State Forces Alliance, Ammar Al-Hakim, met with Iranian Minister of Science, Research and Technology Hossein Simaei Sarraf in Baghdad to discuss expanding academic cooperation between Iraq and Iran through university partnerships, knowledge exchange, and joint educational initiatives.

The meeting focused on strengthening higher education ties while emphasizing the role of universities in addressing labor market needs and societal challenges.

According to a statement released by Al-Hakim’s office, the two sides reviewed opportunities to deepen cooperation between Iraqi and Iranian universities by promoting twinning agreements, expanding academic collaboration, and exchanging expertise.

The discussions highlighted the importance of strengthening institutional relationships to support scientific research and educational development in both countries.

During the meeting, Al-Hakim stressed that university graduates should possess skills that match the demands of today’s job market.

He also urged academic institutions to prioritize scientific research that offers practical solutions to national challenges and contributes to sustainable development.

Al-Hakim emphasized the importance of equipping university students with strong scientific knowledge to prepare them for future professional opportunities.

The Iraqi political leader underscored the role of research institutions in supporting innovation and policymaking.

He noted that universities should focus on producing research capable of addressing economic, social, and developmental issues while enhancing academic excellence.

The discussion reflected a shared interest in strengthening educational cooperation as part of broader bilateral relations.

The meeting also touched on the annual Arbaeen pilgrimage, with Al-Hakim praising the hospitality shown by Iraqis toward visitors traveling to commemorate Imam Hussein.

He said the event demonstrates positive values of solidarity and cooperation, while calling for stronger ties between societies based on shared humanitarian and religious principles.

The visit concluded with discussions on enhancing educational cooperation alongside broader people-to-people engagement between Iraq and Iran.

World.title: Iraq’s State Administration Coalition warns armed groups after September 30
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s State Administration Coalition has reaffirmed its support for restricting all weapons to state control, warning that any armed activity outside the authority of the government after September 30, 2026, will be treated under the country’s Anti-Terrorism Law.

The position was announced following the coalition’s 37th regular meeting, hosted by Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi, with the participation of Iraq’s senior political and constitutional leaders.

According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office, the meeting brought together the President of the Republic, the Speaker of Parliament, the President of the Supreme Judicial Council, the President of the Kurdistan Region, and leaders of the State Administration Coalition.

Participants reviewed Iraq’s political, security, economic, and public service developments, as well as regional events and their impact on the country.

The coalition reiterated its backing for the government’s efforts to ensure that all weapons remain under state authority, in line with the government program approved by the Iraqi Parliament.

The coalition stressed that Iraqi territory must not be used as a launchpad for attacks against neighboring countries or for actions that could draw Iraq into regional conflicts.

It warned that individuals or groups engaging in such activities would be committing crimes that threaten national security.

According to the statement, after September 30, 2026, any armed activity conducted outside the state’s legal framework will be dealt with under Iraq’s Anti-Terrorism Law.

Officials also cited constitutional provisions prohibiting the formation of armed organizations outside the official security forces.

Prime Minister Al-Zaidi briefed coalition members on government efforts to strengthen security, improve public services, implement the ministerial program, and address Iraq’s financial and economic challenges.

The coalition emphasized the need to:

Maintain national security and stability.

Protect essential public services.

Diversify Iraq’s oil export routes.

Increase non-oil revenues.

Combat corruption, smuggling, and financial waste.

The meeting highlighted the government’s commitment to protecting citizens’ interests while strengthening economic resilience.

On regional affairs, coalition leaders expressed support for diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions across the Middle East.

The meeting reaffirmed Iraq’s rejection of resolving disputes through military force and emphasized Baghdad’s willingness to play a constructive role in promoting dialogue between regional parties.

Participants also discussed border security, counterterrorism cooperation, combating drug trafficking and organized crime, and strengthening relations with neighboring and international partners based on mutual respect and national sovereignty.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the State Administration Coalition called for accelerating the completion of the government formation process and submitting the government’s official program to the Council of Representatives for discussion and approval.

The coalition said completing these constitutional steps remains essential for advancing Iraq’s political stability and governance agenda.

World.title: 'Internal matter for us': MEA dismisses US lawmaker's criticism of FCRA Bill
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Friday rejected criticism of India's foreign funding law, saying the issue is an internal matter on which Parliament will take a decision.

During a bi-weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said several countries, including the United States, regulate foreign funds and foreign financing.

"Regarding the issue you are referring to, we have seen it, and several comments have been made on it. As far as legislative matters are concerned, and particularly matters relating to India's own legislation, this is an internal matter for us, on which our Parliament takes the decision," Jaiswal said.

"I would also like to tell you that there are several countries in the world, including the United States, that regulate foreign funds and foreign financing," he added.

The remarks came days after a US lawmaker criticised the proposed amendments to India's foreign funding law, alleging they could allow the government to take over churches and religious charities and warning that the issue could affect India-US ties.





US Congressman Riley Moore said the proposed changes to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) amounted to "a clear attack against Christians" and urged India not to proceed with the legislation in its current form.

In a post on X, the Republican Congressman from West Virginia said Christianity had a long history in India dating back to the arrival of St Thomas the Apostle on the Malabar Coast.

"But despite this long Christian history, India's Parliament is considering amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act to permit government takeovers of churches and religious charities," Moore wrote.

"This is a clear attack against Christians. If this bill proceeds in this way, it would be a point of major concern in our bilateral relationship with India," he added.

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 proposes the creation of a Designated Authority to take over the management of foreign contributions and assets created using such funds if an organisation's FCRA registration is cancelled, surrendered or lapses after not being renewed.

The Bill specifies that where such assets include a place of worship, the Designated Authority must ensure its religious character is preserved.

It also proposes reducing the maximum punishment for violations of the Act from five years' imprisonment to one year.

The FCRA regulates the receipt and utilisation of foreign contributions by NGOs, charitable trusts, educational institutions, religious bodies and other associations. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, 13,520 organisations received foreign contributions worth Rs 55,741 crore between 2019 and 2022.

Government data shows that as of July 15, 2026, there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations, while 22,498 had been cancelled and another 15,212 had expired.

World.title: Suresh Narayanan’s leadership book signals the death of the ‘charismatic’ CEO; urges India Inc to shed elitism crutch
World.content:
Former Nestle CMD Suresh Narayanan in his new book, 'Courage Under Fire', writes that in a crisis people follow those they trust.

For over four decades,

Suresh Narayanan

has navigated boardrooms, brand battles and one of

India Inc

's defining crises. In â

Courage Under Fire

â (

Penguin Random House India

), the former NestlÃ© India chairman and managing director looks beyond business strategy to explore what truly shapes

leadership

.

In an exclusive chat with Lopamudra Ghatak, he argues that clarity matters more than charisma, challenges India's obsession with pedigree thatâs causing companies to overlook leadership potential, and reflects candidly on the lessons of the

Maggi

crisis. He also explains why

Gen Z

's approach to work-life balance deserves respect rather than ridicule, and recalls how a woman boss taught him that empathy is one of the key traits to being a good leader.

Congratulations on your book. How did the idea to write 'Courage Under Fire' come to you?

In 'Courage Under Fire' you write that "great leadership is not about position; itâs about responsibility, authenticity, and the ability to inspire trust, when it matters". In an increasingly trust-deficit and information-surplus world, how does a leader earn trust? And how does an organisation make trust a part of its DNA?

'Performative' is the word that's often used today ...

mukhota

Trust is the real currency of leadership.(Image generated by AI)

This bring me to my next question: Can leadership be taught, or is it something people are simply born with?

Nestle India CMD Suresh Narayanan (File photo)

That's an interesting point about the 'charisma myth' that surrounds

leadership. You mention in the book about visiting Tier-2 and Tier3- colleges, and how students there are often more grateful, hungry and eager to learn. Do you think they make better leaders?

The 'tag' matters?

Why great leaders don't need charisma(Image generated by AI)

You have spent over four decades across big brands. Do you think India Inc has begun to move beyond that elitism?

The modern workplace has become very volatile, with geopolitics and global uncertainty adding new layers of complexity. What's your advice for leaders navigating crises?

What should I say? How should I behave? What tone should I set?

In hindsight, do you feel that your response to the Maggi crisis was appropriate? Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

In 'Courage Under Fire', you write about the emotional effect the loss of colleagues during the pandemic had on you. Do you think business leaders, particularly men, are becoming more comfortable showing their vulnerable side?

You also had a woman boss during your career. Did her leadership style differ from your male mentors?

Gen Z and the emerging Gen Alpha are reshaping workplace expectations as they place a premium on work-life balance, purpose and flexibility. How do you see that influencing India's workforce in the years ahead?

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

After a 40-year career in corporate India, I wanted to leave behind a few lessons that had served me well. They're not prescriptions, but perspectives shaped by the crises and difficult moments I have experienced.'Courage Under Fire' is more of a personal journey through those defining moments - that focuses on people, purpose, partnerships, values, behaviour and outcomes. I thought it would be of some use to a younger generation entering the workforce.I think you've hit the nail on the head! Trust is the most valuable currency - for an individual as much as for an organisation. It emerges when three streams converge at one point in time.The first is purpose. Every organisation, and every individual, needs a clear sense of purpose, something that guides decisions and actions.The second is values. What do you want to be known for? What principles define how you conduct yourself, especially in adverse situations?Purpose and values, in turn, lead to the third element: authenticity. Unfortunately, in today's digital world, authenticity often gives way to performance.We spend too much time embellishing, instead of being genuine.Correct. Leadership isn't about saying what you'll do, it's about doing what you say. That's the dilemma many leaders face. Do they wear a(mask) that projects one image while concealing another?In order to establish trust among people, there has to be a convergence between purpose, values and authenticity, and that leads to outcomes. Over time, those actions create credibility, and credibility becomes trust.Trust is built when purpose, values and authenticity consistently translate into action. Over time, those actions create credibility, and credibility becomes trust.I've also come to see vulnerability as a strength, not a weakness. When people know you're human, that you have strengths as well as limitations, they know what to expect from you. Predictability in values and behaviour is reassuring. What people fear most is unpredictability.Ultimately, trust isn't about being the most liked person in the room. In a crisis, organisations don't rely on the most loved people; they rely on the most trusted ones. If I'm liked but not trusted, I won't be asked to lead when it matters. Trust, more than popularity, is what carries an organisation through difficult times.Leadership, for long, has suffered from some myths. The first is the myth of charisma - that great leaders must have magnetic personalities. The second is that complex communication (by leadership) is somehow superior. The third is executive presence: the belief that a leader must be a larger-than-life figure at any gathering and dominate every room they enter. And the fourth is the idea that leaders should only display their strengths while hiding every flaw, angularities.I don't subscribe to any of those myths. Leadership can absolutely be taught because, at its core, leadership is an act of being human.You don't have to be charismatic; you have to be clear. You don't have to be complex; you have to be transparent in your communication. You don't need the loudest voice or the most commanding presence. Some of history's greatest political and business leaders inspired people far beyond the reach of their voices.But leadership doesn't develop in isolation. It blooms through the right mentors, timely nudges and experiences. Looking back, I benefited from teachers, parents, colleagues, relatives and even competitors who pushed me to exceed my own expectations. Those influences gradually built confidence, not just the confidence to lead others, but the confidence to manage myself first.One thing we need to do as a society is demystify elitism. We place far too much value on where someone studied, where they work, the company they built or the organisation they belong to â as though those labels alone define success and achievement.Exactly, the tag culture. I believe those days should be behind us. Look at ISRO. They might have their own travails but the fact is that most of the talent that comes there are not from the premier institutions in the country and yet they do premier and outstanding work and make us proud as a nation.The same is true of organisations that consciously recruit from Tier-2 cities and smaller towns. I often find students there to be remarkably humble, eager and determined. They are trying to prove themselves against a system that has long suggested only the elite succeed.As leaders, we have to move away from that entitlement mindset and create space for talent to flourish. India has extraordinary talent. Some young people may not be the most articulate when speaking in English but they are capable of hard work and possess grit, discipline and can deliver on their promise each and every time.That's what the country needsânot people who merely preach from the pulpit, but people who consistently deliver.I think as a country now we are mature enough to realise that we cannot be a developing country or hope to become a wealthy country one day on the crutches of elitism. I think elitism is a crutch that we have to get out of as quickly as possible.I think the kind of companies that I worked in - Unilever, Colgate-Palmolive and Nestle - they always prided themselves in a middle-class culture. Their leaders weren't chosen because they came from privileged backgrounds; they rose through competence, commitment, energy and hard workI use the term middle class in a positive sense because it symbolises humility, integrity, transparency, trust and a strong work ethic. This is what middle-class India is, and these are the values we strive to teach our children. When those values enter an organisation, they become a source of strength.I do think the growing recognition of talent from Tier-2 institutions and smaller towns is slowly weakening elitism. But there's still work to be done. Our education system and employers must create more opportunities for capable graduates from less celebrated institutions.Too many people still believe admission to a top college guarantees success. Life doesn't work that way. Success is usually about moving two steps forward, one step back, and repeating that journey with resilience and consistency.There are two principles that have guided me throughout my career.The first is simple: a crisis never arrives with a calling card. You have to remain alert at all times. Don't be caught sleeping at the wheel. Anticipate risks before they balloon into crises.The second is to manage yourself before you manage others. That's often overlooked. When a crisis hits, we immediately focus on facts, meetings and firefighting. But we spend far less time asking:In a crisis, everyone's anxiety levels are elevated. The leader's role is to remain calm, anchored in the organisation's purpose and values, and provide stability.That's often the difference between a crisis handled well and one handled badly. The outcome rarely depends only on strategy. More often, it depends on leadershipâhow clearly you communicate, how consistently you act and how much confidence you inspire.The first lesson, that a crisis doesn't come with a calling card, certainly applies in this case. In hindsight, we could have done better in terms of sensing the environment and knowing that something was brewing in parts of the country. If we had been able to address it more comprehensively, maybe we would have been able to manage the outcome a lot better.Secondly, one of the important issues in managing a crisis is to have a single point of contact communicating to the environment. One criticism we faced was that we were slow in communicating. Looking back, I believe we could have responded faster.I don't know whether the dial has shifted enough in India to say that with confidence. But I do believe people follow leaders who are authentic, humane and emotionally present â not those who remain distant and issue instructions from above.Professor George Kohlrieser at IMD Business School describes a leader as a "secure base." I find that idea deeply meaningful. Just as we turn to a parent in moments of uncertainty, employees should feel they have someone they can approach with their fears, concerns and aspirations, someone who will provide anchorage in a crisis.Vulnerability, to me, is a source of strength. It acknowledges that you're still learning and growing. That's not weakness, it's humanity.We've long been told that men don't cry. But they do. Suppressing emotion doesn't make you stronger; it makes it harder to empathise. And empathy is one of the most powerful qualities a leader can possess.Wan Ling, who headed Nestle Asia-Oceania-Africa, was one of the toughest leaders I worked with. She could be incredibly demanding, yet deeply compassionate.What struck me most was that every conversation with her began with family. With many of my male bosses, business came first and family last. With her it was always, âHow is your family doing?â. Only then would we move on to tackle the toughest business crisis moments.One of her greatest strengths was her ability to read a room. She sensed what people were feeling before anyone uttered a word. Just as importantly, she had the ability to step back, consider various perspectives and avoid rushing into decisions. That balance of empathy and judgement made her an exceptional leader.I see it as a positive shift. The old belief that success demanded 80-hour work weeks came at a huge personal cost. You may have earned more, but you often missed out on family, friendships and life's important moments. There's little value in reaching 80 and regretting that you never spent enough time with your parents or your children. So I welcome this change.These youngsters are not work-shy. They simply want work to coexist with life, and I think that's a healthy aspiration. I only wish my generation had the courage to tell our bosses at seven in the evening that we were leaving to meet family or friends. Instead, we stayed back until the boss switched off the lights, as though commitment was measured by the last person to leave the office.That said, balance has to be calibrated. Every generation has something to learn from the other.What also strikes me about young professionals is that they're driven by experiences. They move from one challenge to another in search of learning and fulfillment. I would encourage them to embrace the challenge itself rather than becoming overly anxious about the outcome. Careers are rarely linear. If you focus on learning, growth and doing meaningful work, the outcomes usually take care of themselves.

World.title: 'News, Spice Rani, He Ram': Names on police merit list triggers row in Chhattisgarh
World.content:
NEW DELHI: What began as a routine police recruitment result in Chhattisgarh quickly turned into an internet sensation after candidates with names such as 'News', 'Space Rani', 'He Ram', 'Bhakt Prahlad' and 'Tufail' appeared on the list of successful applicants, sparking disbelief, political allegations and eventually, a defence from the candidates themselves.

The unusual names, which surfaced in the results of the Chhattisgarh Public Service Commission's (CGPSC) preliminary examination for police recruitment, prompted the opposition Congress to question the credibility of the selection process.

The commission, however, dismissed the allegations, insisting that the names were genuine and matched the details submitted by candidates during registration.

What really happened

The controversy erupted after the results of the preliminary examination for 341 posts of subedar, sub-inspector and platoon commander were declared on August 4.

A total of 7,301 candidates qualified for the mains examination.

According to the CGPSC, the candidates had appeared for document verification, physical tests and the preliminary examination under the same names, which were also printed on their admit cards.

Former chief minister Bhupesh Baghel mocked the list after sharing it on X.

"The Public Relations Department should spend Rs 1 crore daily on s to display this achievement at public intersections so that, in the coming days, 'Radio' and 'Space Raja' might also succeed in some examination."





State Congress communication wing chief Sushil Anand Shukla accused the BJP government of failing to deliver transparent recruitment despite promising PSC examinations on the lines of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC).

He alleged that the names reflected the alleged "negligence" of the CGPSC and the state government and claimed that several recruitment and promotion examinations held over the past two-and-a-half years had come under suspicion.

What the board said

Rejecting the allegations, the CGPSC described the claims circulating on social media as "misleading and baseless" and said they unfairly ridiculed candidates over their names.

"The names of the candidates displayed in the examination result are the same as those entered by them in their online application forms, which they finally submitted. The candidates appeared for document and physical tests as well as the preliminary examination under these names, and their names were also displayed accordingly on their admit cards," it stated.

The commission urged candidates and the public not to believe misinformation and rely only on information published on its official website.

Several candidates clarify

As the debate gathered pace online, several candidates clarified that the names attracting attention were the same as those recorded in their official documents.

"My name is News Kumar Pradhan. My surname was not added to my Class 10 marksheet. My marksheets of Classes 10 and 12 and Aadhaar card carry the name News, without the surname.

People think that the name is incorrect," said News Kumar Pradhan, who qualified in the preliminary examination. He added that he is from Bhatanpali village in Raigarh district.

Tufail, a 29-year-old candidate from Nayapara in Raipur district, said his name appeared the same in all official records.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"After the result was released, rumours are being spread about names such as Spacerani, News and Tufail without any information or facts.

These are the names of students who have prepared for the examination for years," he said.

He appealed against spreading rumours and said such claims were hurting the morale of candidates from ordinary families.

Another successful candidate, He Ram, said there was nothing unusual about the way his name was recorded.

"My name is He Ram, and I have qualified the PSC preliminary examination. Some people are raising objections over my name. My surname is Kashyap, but it is not mentioned in any of my documents. Hence, I entered only my name while filling the form," he told PTI.

Bhakt Prahlad also clarified that his name was correctly recorded in all official documents.

"My surname is not mentioned. Please do not spread confusion regarding my name," he said.

World.title: Sukhbir Singh Badal meets PM Modi, fuels BJP-SAD alliance buzz ahead of Punjab polls next year
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

(SAD) chief

met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Parliament on Friday. The meeting has sparked buzz over whether the BJP and the SAD are preparing to turn the page on years of political estrangement ahead of the

For both the BJP and the SAD, the timing is significant. Once the state's dominant political combine, the two parties have spent the past several years on the margins of Punjab politics, watching their traditional support base shrink while Kejriwal-led

The BJP-SAD who were allies for over two decades, parted ways in September 2020 after the Akali Dal walked out of the

NDA

, with much credits to Centre's three farm laws. The legislation triggered massive protests across Punjab and countrywide and became a political flashpoint.

However, even after PM Modi-led government repealed the laws in 2021, relations between the two allies remained strained.

In the 2022 Punjab assembly elections, voters not only rejected the Congress, which was crippled by the Amarinder Singh-Navjot Singh Sidhu power struggle, but also delivered a crushing verdict against both the BJP and the SAD.

Contesting separately, the BJP won just two seats while the Akali Dal managed only three in the 117-member assembly.





Instead, Punjab handed Kejriwal's AAP a historic mandate. The party stormed to power for the first time in its second attempt, with Bhagwant Mann becoming chief minister, recording a dramatic shift in the Sikh-majority state.

World.title: Uttarakhand Forward 2.0 | Manoj Pant maps out development roadmap to 2047

Uttarakhand Forward 2.0 is the second edition of The Times of India's flagship video series spotlighting the state's journey of growth, innovation and transformative governance.

As India moves towards the centenary of its independence in 2047, the discussion examines what it will take for Uttarakhand to emerge as a resilient, sustainable, and future-ready state over the next two decades.

World.title: Govt bars firms filing fake drug data from seeking fresh approvals
World.content:
Govt bars firms filing fake drug data from seeking fresh approvals. (Photo: IANS)

NEW DELHI:

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

In a major crackdown on regulatory fraud in the pharmaceutical sector, the Centre has amended the Drugs Rules, 1945 to empower drug regulators to temporarily debar companies that submit fake or fabricated data while seeking approvals for drugs and related licences.Under the amended rules notified by the Union health ministry on Thursday, applicants found submitting fabricated data will not only face rejection of their applications or cancellation of existing licences, but can also be barred from filing fresh applications before the concerned licensing authority, whether at the Centre or in the states, for a specified period. The action will be taken only after issuing a show-cause notice, and affected applicants will have the right to appeal.The new provision will apply to all applications filed under the Drugs Rules, 1945, and is aimed at deterring companies from submitting false scientific data to secure regulatory approvals.The ministry said regulatory decisions on the quality, safety and efficacy of medicines are based on scientific data submitted by applicants. Fabricated data undermines the integrity of the approval process, raises questions about the quality of medicines and can pose serious risks to public health.The amendment is intended to strengthen accountability and ensure that drug approvals are backed by reliable scientific evidence.Officials said the amendment is part of the government's broader effort to align India's drug regulatory framework with global best practices by promoting ethical compliance while taking stricter action against companies that indulge in malpractice.

World.title: Karthik Manikandan’s ‘Enam’ explores the inner life of Maricha, the golden deer in ‘The Ramayana’
World.content:
Maricha the charming golden deer appears only for a few fleeting moments in The Ramayana. But his story endures. Born to the demoness Tataka, Maricha’s life arc begins and ends with Rama. Ever since Rama’s arrow kills his brother Subahu, Maricha has nurtured a simmering grudge against Rama. It was only logical then to agree when his nephew Ravana sought his help in his grand ploy to abduct Sita. Because deep down, in his heart, he knew he wanted to die at Rama’s hands.

These contradictions in Maricha’s character come beautifully alive in Enam, a dance theatre production by Bharatanatyam artiste Karthik Manikandan. He transforms into deer with deft movements and expressions. Enam, Karthik’s first solo production, shows off his strengths as a dancer and actor. Having learnt Kathakali as well, Karthik blends various elements of dance and drama to build an engaging narrative.

“When you begin to think of it, Maricha is a fascinating character. Flitting through the forest, a flash of gold in the darkness of the trees, he lures Rama deeper into the woods, crying out for Lakshmana in Rama’s voice, in a final act of treachery. I wanted to explore the many shades of the character,” he says.

A blend of styles

Karthik’s choreography blends various elements — the jatis of Bharatanatyam, the slokas in the style of Kathalaki padas and a hint of folk music such as sarpam thullal (a traditional ritual art performed to appease snake Gods). “When I was thinking of producing my own piece, I had Hidimbi, the powerful asura character from The Mahabharata in mind. But it was dancer Manju V Nair who suggested Maricha. The idea appealed to me and I started reading up, and trying to understand the various nuances,” says Karthik.

The one-hour-50 minute piece took seven months to achieve its current form, he says. While the music has been composed by Uduppi Srinath, the lyrics have been penned by Vellinezhi Harikrishnan (who is also a Kathakali artiste) in Manipravalam.

Karthik’s Maricha is playful, intense and cunning all at once. “When he sees Sita for the first time, he is awestruck by her beauty. He plays with Sita, enchanting her with his grace and charm. But soon he transforms into the cunning demon when he spots Rama,” says Karthik.

Born and brought up in Kallekkulangara, Palakkad, Karthik has been learning dance from a very young age. Currently learning Bharatanatyam under Parshwanath Upadhye, Shruti Gopal and Adithya PV at the Upadhye School of Dance in Bengaluru, Karthik aims to focus on Bharatanatyam.

Karthik has performed Enam across stages in Kerala and outside.

World.title: ‘Korean Kanakaraju’ review: Varun Tej and Sathya’s comic timing cannot rescue this dull narrative
World.content:
Telugu cinema has repeatedly turned to the horror-comedy genre to deliver crowd-pleasers. Often, a handful of genuinely funny stretches have been enough to carry narratives that are otherwise uneven. As long as the laughs land, audiences have been willing to overlook the rest. Director Merlapaka Gandhi returns to this familiar template, this time throwing K-dramas and K-pop into the mix in the hope of lending the genre a fresh twist.

The premise of Korean Kanakaraju is intriguing. The ashes of a Korean man somehow end up in an unassuming bar in Andhra Pradesh's Anantapur district. Through a bizarre turn of events, Kanakaraju (Varun Tej) accidentally mixes alcohol with the ashes, drinks it and becomes possessed.

What follows is a tug-of-war between Kanakaraju and the Korean spirit inhabiting him. The Anantapur setting also allows the film to tap into the region's association with a major Korean automobile manufacturer, tying into Chaitra's (Ritika Nayak) dream of visiting Korea and her fascination with K-pop and K-dramas. Before long, the story attempts to bring together Rayalaseema machismo and Korean gang wars, with Kanakaraju's hapless friend Kistappa (Sathya) caught in the crossfire.

Korean Kanakaraju (Telugu) Director: Merlapaka Gandhi Cast: Varun Tej Konidela, Ritika Nayak, Sathya Runtime: 165 minutes Storyline: What happens when a man in Anantapur is possessed by a Korean spirit and has to reclaim his identity

The film takes over 45 minutes to arrive at its central conflict. That would not have been a problem had the opening stretch been engaging. Instead, Kanakaraju’s introduction, his family dynamics, the romance and the local rivalries are all written in a generic fashion, padded further by songs that barely leave an impression.

Korean Kanakaraju finally comes alive once Kanakaraju is possessed. A few pre-interval sequences, particularly those set in a factory, are handled with flair. Animal lovers, however, may find the subplot involving a pet dog named Jung Kook and its fate difficult to stomach. The film plays it for morbid humour, but it may not work for everyone.

The narrative gathers momentum once the action shifts to Korea and Kanakaraju, Chaitra and Kistappa begin to understand what they are up against. It helps, of course, if you don’t stop to wonder why the Korean police are nowhere to be seen.

Beyond a handful of twists, the gangster drama does not soar. A comic subplot featuring VTV Ganesh and child actor Revanth also fails to land.

The standout moment in the latter half is a genuinely funny sequence involving Kistappa and his father (Muralidhar Goud), whose video call is repeatedly disrupted by poor mobile connectivity.

Beyond that, the film overstays its welcome. The visual effects are unconvincing, and the VFX-heavy climax is neither imaginative nor exciting in execution.

Korean Kanakaraju leans heavily on Sathya’s comic timing, and he delivers, as always. But there is only so much heavy lifting he can do when the writing lets him down. Varun Tej is sincere as a man caught between two personalities, but the film never gives us enough reason to invest in his predicament. Ritika Nayak does what she can with a limited role, while Srinivas Avasarala makes a brief appearance that adds a touch of gravitas.

By the time the drawn-out climax finally ends, it is hard to care about either the man possessed, or the one leaving destruction in his wake.

World.title: Too big to be cozy: the BJP’s expansion plans have problems and they are showing
World.content:
In a marathon four-hour meeting at Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s residence a few weeks ago, in the presence of senior leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), including Union Home Minister Amit Shah, BJP president Nitin Nabin, RSS joint general secretary Arun Kumar among others, the Sangh Parivar mulled over its HR (human resources) issues.

The BJP, which has seen an unprecedented growth not just electorally but also organisationally, with recruits from other parties and its own growth, faced the fact that its organisational structure needed expanding to accommodate old-timers and new entrants. The meeting drew up a blueprint to increase the number of organisational posts to satisfy all.

The result of the Bankipur bypoll in Bihar, where the BJP lost its fort in the heart of Patna, has also signalled the discontent of that expansion, this time in its support base.

The past 12 years have seen an unprecedented rise of the BJP, a matter of satisfaction for any political party. It has also seen the party grow far beyond what used to be its ideological and organisational comfort zones.

The Bankipur poll loss of the BJP is being seen as a rearguard action by the party’s core upper caste support base upset over its interests being neglected in favour of consolidating the BJP’s now-formidable OBC vote bank. The UGC social equity regulations, the killing of social activist Bharat Tiwari allegedly by Bihar Police, and the very appointment of Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary – who, despite having migrated to the BJP via the RJD and the JD(U), landed the top job for which thousands of BJP workers had slogged – led to the cocktail of reasons for the BJP’s loss.

Bihar is not the only geography where the newbies versus old-timers issue has played. In Maharashtra, during the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, BJP workers and RSS members refused to campaign for the NCP (Ajit) candidates citing years of political rivalry on the ground and bitter feelings. Months later, during the Assembly polls, the BJP, NCP (Ajit) and the RSS gelled together as the implications of the 2024 Lok Sabha tally of 240 seats were brought home.

In West Bengal, the accommodation of Trinamool MPs and workers in the BJP after decades of violent face-offs on the ground has led to even senior leaders like Dilip Ghosh express apprehensions over the dilution of both cadre zeal and ideology in the newly won State.

As with everything, for the BJP, this expansion of its ideological footprint has not been without its costs – upsetting old-timers, diluting some ideological principles (as in the case of turning a blind eye to beef consumption in Kerala and the Northeastern States) and now, an upper caste disenchantment that has the capacity to hit at the core of its support base.

On the positive side, the BJP has become a big umbrella party for a large section of people and a significant geographical spread. As with all empires, however, authority is never weaker than at its strongest and most expansive, with many mutinies, from the young, the old-timers, the upper castes and those at the geographical margins of this spread.

For the BJP, the Bankipur bypoll loss and the GenZ protests have brought home forcefully that it is now too big to be cosy, its government has been too long at the helm to be given benefit of doubt by long-suffering party men and women awaiting accommodation and opportunity, and that the expansion of an ideological footprint can also result in dilution of first principles.

World.title: Supreme Court refuses to entertain Mahua Moitra's plea against appearing before police in hate speech case
World.content:
The Supreme Court on Friday (August 7, 2026) refused to entertain a plea by Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra challenging an order of the Calcutta High Court directing her to appear before the police on August 15 in a hate speech case.

A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said it was not inclined to interfere with the High Court order.

Senior advocate Gopal Sankarnarayanan, appearing for the MP, submitted that she has a legal right under law to appear virtually before the police.

"The requirement as per the police's notice is to be at the police station in my own constituency. Last time I went there two things happened. First there were threats that eggs will be thrown etc. and second time eggs were actually thrown," he said.

Asking her to appear before police, the Bench observed orally, "You are a Member of Parliament. Having taken the plunge into politics, you fear eggs?

"When our freedom fighters have taken bullets on their chest? These are applications that should not come before this court at all," the Bench said.

As the Bench was not inclined to entertain the matter, the senior lawyer withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.

The Calcutta High Court on July 21 had granted interim protection from coercive action to Ms. Moitra till October 5 in a hate speech case which she claimed is based on fabricated charges.

The Krishnanagar MP prayed before the court for an interim order preventing coercive police action in the case and quashing of proceedings against her in the case registered at Hogolberia police station in Nadia district.

Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya of the High Court had directed Ms. Moitra to appear before the investigating officer on August 14 for questioning in the case.

The court had directed that no coercive steps be taken against her till October 5 subject to compliance with the conditions alluded to until October or until further order, whichever is earlier.

Noting that the BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) provisions applied to Moitra carry a maximum punishment below seven years, the court had observed that she is entitled to protection from coercive action provided she cooperates with the investigation.

Justice Bhattacharyya had directed Ms. Moitra to cooperate with the probe and comply with police notices by appearing before the investigating officer.

The court directed that the matter will be heard again on October 1.

World.title: Tamil Nadu’s expectation of higher Central funds pushes up total revenue receipts
World.content:
The Tamil Nadu government’s expectation of more funds from the Union government has revised upwards the estimated amount of total revenue receipts (TRR) for the current year.

In the past three out of five years, the budget estimates for the TRR were pushed down at the time of arriving at the revised estimates. On the contrary, this time, the TRR figure is higher by ₹5,452 crore over the budget estimate’s figure. Compared to ₹3,44,575 crore provided at the time of the presentation of the budget figure earlier this year, the State government has calculated that the TRR will be ₹3,50,027 crore.

The increase in funds will be an outcome of the State government’s participation in the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB G RAM-G), according to a perusal of the revised budget documents for 2026-27. This is being reflected in the Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), which will see a rise of about ₹9,790 crore.

As the new rural job guarantee scheme requires a contribution of 40% by the State government, there will be an outgo of ₹5,057 crore from the State’s kitty, even as there will be an inflow of ₹7,586 crore. In addition, an amount of ₹3,461 crore is due to the State under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), the precursor to VB G RAM-G. These explain the increase in the revised amount under the head of the CSS.

The White Paper, presented by the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led regime in June, spoke of budget credibility gap and revenue receipts falling short of projections in the past. On the contrary, the maiden budget of the current regime presents a contrasting picture, at least with regard to the TRR.

Apart from VB G RAM-G causing the increase in the CSS figure, the answer had to be inferred from the Budget speech of Finance Minister N. Marie Wilson, who referred to various measures being taken by his government for additional resource mobilisation, as a result of which approximately ₹15,000 crore is expected. This includes ₹3,250 crore from mines to be facilitated by end-to-end computerisation in monitoring mining activity; the levy of additional privilege fee on liquor manufacturers; and leveraging Information Technology through ‘faceless assessment’ under the Goods and Services Tax; and ‘faceless registration’ in the Registration Department.

World.title: How memories and motifs inspire Onam 2026 collections
World.content:
A classic Malayalam film song, a fleeting Onam memory, the flowers that suddenly fill up our courtyards, the comforting feeling of being at home ... designers are spotlighting fresh perspectives and imagery related to Onam in their new collections.

Pulari — Rouka by Sreejith Jeevan

Designer Sreejith Jeevan of Rouka calls the collection he has launched for Onam Pulari, which means dawn in Malayalam. Inspiration was the Malayalam song Thiruvona Pulari, by Vani Jayaram, but of course, the collection has the signature Rouka ‘quirk factor’ or, as Sreejith calls it, “nostalgia with a quirky interpretation.” So the collection has the Kerala landscape, backwaters, coconut palm-lined roads, among other elements, apart from the fauna and flora of the State.

Although the collection has come out around Onam, he makes a point about conscious consumption, because festival shopping tends to get a tad mindless.

Sustainability has been a big part of the designer Sreejith Jeevan’s design philosophy; repurposing and versatility also feature prominently. “Over the past decade or so, we designers have been thinking — ‘what is sustainability?’ It is how you shop, wear and repurpose,” he says. What he suggests is rather to shop for ‘sustainable’ options and make it a practice.

He illustrates his point with the example of the number of Onam events a person might have to attend. “Rather than buying 13 looks for each event, buy little pieces that can be repurposed and used differently.” Like his his mundu-duppatta concept, for instance, a departure from the white and gold of Onam. Both can be used later and be worn differently, all year round.

Shop for this collection at shoprouka.com

The Hands Behind Onam — Pranaah

Pranaah’s Onam 2026 is a burst of colours. Founder of the label and designer Poornima Indrajith says she wanted something that reflected the spirit of the season without “screaming it”. “It had to be different, yet it had to capture the essence of Onam,” she says.

Hours of brainstorming later, Poornima knew what her collection would be. “The hands behind Onam… The festival is all about flowers and we decided to trace the flowers that are used in pookkalams, which is the main part of the festivities – where they come from, where the markets are, the people who work in these markets…. The collection is an appreciation for the hands behind the celebration,” she says.

This led her to the flower markets of Coimbatore. It didn’t take long for her to translate the small mounds of flowers, people and bustle of a market into wearable works of art. A design, Pooncholai, has petals of the flowers arali, jamanthi and more interpreted in handloom in Pranaah’s signature embroidery. Poornima, however, didn’t want to limit her collection to handloom this time. She uses prints on organza too, in a range titled Poovasantham. “Organza is such a breezy, flowy fabric and with all of these floral motifs, they can also be styled and worn to a cocktail party,” says Poornima. The palette isn’t all cream either – there’s peach, red, brown, yellow, brown and orange, ensuring that the garments can be worn through the year. The collection includes saris, salwar kurtas and shirts.

Available at Pranaah store in Panampilly Nagar and pranaah.com

Orma — House of Urmi

The House of Urmi derives its Onam collection from memory or Orma, a tribute to the cherished memories of old-world Onam. “This year’s Onam collection is our interpretation of the simple, nostalgic Onam that many of us grew up hearing about or experienced. Instead of focusing on grand festive elements, I wanted to celebrate the quieter moments, the joy of making pookkalam together, children on swings, women dancing, blooming Krishna kireedam flowers, parrots, and the lush landscapes that make Kerala so special,” says the founder, Anjali.

The Kerala-inspired House of Urmi prints begin as original painted artworks, created by Anjali. These are then digitally printed onto fabric and finished with embroidery, which adds depth and texture.

“Through these motifs, the idea was to tell little stories of old-world Onam and preserve that warmth and innocence in a contemporary, wearable form.

The collection goes beyond saris to include printed crop tops that can be styled as blouses or worn on their own, Kerala-inspired shirts for men, and contemporary dresses featuring the same original painted prints. The idea was to create versatile festive wear that can be enjoyed during Onam and beyond. The saris are crafted in premium cotton, as it offers the ideal base to bring out the intricacy of the original hand-painted artworks with exceptional clarity and colour,” Anjali adds.

Shop this collection at houseofurmi.in

Ivory Edit — Yarn Culture

Yarn Culture’s Onam collection, every year, is called the Ivory Edit. This year, however, says Sayujya Sajilal, of the online store, that collection did not begin with a colour, a fabric or a trend. “It began with a memory. The idea was simple: the feeling of home during Onam. Rain collecting in the courtyard, the familiar sound of an old swing, flowers picked in the morning and left in a brass vessel before the house wakes up. These are small moments many Malayalis have grown up with, and they became the starting point for the collection,” she says.

The custom-designed saris, inspired by memories – Manjadi, Chethi, Mandaram, Thamara and Thamara Kattam – are florals. But, rather than a pookalam, the designer picked elements from the pookalam and built a story around each one. First hand-sketched, it was hand-embroidered later.

Manjadi, for instance, comes from one of the strongest childhood memories. It has tiny, red manjadi seeds embroidered across a sandal-toned Kerala cotton saree, with the motifs running along one side of the drape to keep the design understated while letting the embroidery stand out.

Then there is lotus-inspired Thamara Kattam, which is minimal. Small hot pink lotus motifs have been embroidered on a checkered cotton saree; a concept that has been carried into a half-and-half saree, one of the most requested styles this year, where the second half is finished in a vibrant hot pink. For those who want colour in their Onam wardrobe, there are soft cotton Ganga Jamuna sarees. Unlike the traditional Ganga Jamuna saris, Ivory Edit pairs ivory with bold colour combinations including Kanakambaram orange and brown, black and maroon, teal and red, and maroon and green.

Shop this edit at yarnculture.in

World.title: Chef Manjunath Mural brings his Southeast Asian-inspired menu to The Quarter, Chennai
World.content:
This weekend, cocktail bar The Quarter will serve up Southeast Asian flavours as Chef Manjunath Mural presents a special menu of bar bites for Chennai diners. Chef Mural has over two decades of experience leading fine-dining kitchens across India and Singapore.

Chef Manjunath Mural brings an exclusive one-night only menu inspired by his journey across Southeast Asia — designed to be shared over cocktails and conversations. “The chef is usually known for his fine-dining tasting menus, but at The Quarter we’re doing something different,” says Nivruti Reddy, director, Amaravathi Restaurants, which launched the bar earlier this year. “Guests can sample 14 small plates and bar bites in a more relaxed setting.”

Inspired by the chef’s travels across Southeast Asia, the menu celebrates the region’s culinary heritage with dishes such as chicken rendang and murtabak chicken, alongside his signature Singaporean-Indian fusion creations. Expect inventive plates like rojak chaat, Tom Yum Pani Puri, and laksa prawns with lemon leaf upma. The meal ends on a sweet note with a coconut trim cake.

Complementing the menu is a line-up of four Asian-inspired cocktails and two mocktails created for the pop-up. Ingredients such as lemongrass, pandan, galangal and tea take centrestage, while a standout is the mango sticky rice cocktail — a playful take on the classic Southeast Asian dessert.

For Chennai diners, the pop-up offers a rare chance to sample Chef Manjunath Mural’s cuisine in a relaxed cocktail-bar setting, paired with Asian-inspired drinks and small plates designed for sharing. The Quarter is collaborating with Soul on a Plate for this pop-up.

@The Quarter, August 9, 7pm onwards. Entry: ₹2,500 (redeemable) per person. For reservations, call 9841310006.

World.title: Flights from Bhogapuram to foreign destinations very soon, says Kondapalli Srinivas
World.content:
With the inauguration of the Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport at Bhogapuram on August 1 and its scheduled commencement of commercial operations from August 17, flyers from north Andhra Pradesh (Uttarandhra) may soon be able to board flights to various international destinations, including the U.S., Europe and Australia, directly from the new airport.

If things go according to plan, passengers from the region will no longer have to travel to Hyderabad, Chennai, Bengaluru or Mumbai to catch international flights, said Andhra Pradesh Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (SERP) and NRI Empowerment, Kondapalli Srinivas.

In an exclusive interaction with The Hindu, Mr. Srinivas said, “We have about 34 flights operating now, including two international services, one to Abu Dhabi and another to Singapore. There is always scope to increase these numbers. The new airport is not only state-of-the-art but is also equipped to handle large-bodied international aircraft.”

According to the Minister, the Telugu diaspora across the globe is estimated at around 30 lakh, making it one of the largest overseas communities. Of this, around four to five lakh people are believed to hail from Uttarandhra alone. Since the airport has been developed under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model, GMR will play a significant role in promoting its growth and expanding connectivity, he added.

Speaking about domestic expansion, Mr. Srinivas said proposals are already in place for two to three additional flights to Hyderabad and Bengaluru, while services to new destinations such as Coimbatore, Pune and Varanasi are also in the pipeline.

“Our immediate target is to achieve an annual footfall of 50 lakh passengers,” he said.

Catalyst for growth

Mr. Srinivas said the Bhogapuram airport would emerge as a major catalyst for the economic growth of north Andhra. He pointed out that Bhogapuram was chosen because of its strategic location, being almost equidistant from the six districts of Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli, Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram and even Alluri Sitarama Raju district.

“We needed a bigger and more modern airport to meet the growing demands of the region. Airports are catalysts for growth. They not only facilitate passenger movement but also significantly improve cargo logistics,” he said.

The airport is expected to provide a major boost to the transportation of high-value products, including agricultural produce, processed food, pharmaceuticals and, most importantly, the region’s thriving aquaculture exports.

According to the Minister, several major investments are either under way or have shown interest in the region, thanks in part to the improved logistics that the new airport offers.
